articles.title: Exotic animal smuggling baffles activists in India
articles.summary: Orangutans, rare reptiles and other exotic animals are popping up in India, suggesting the country is becoming a major destination for trafficked wildlife.

image.caption: Orangutans in the wild are native only to Indonesia's Sumatra island and Borneo, which it shares with Malaysia and BruneiImage: Odisha Forest Department/AFP

blocks.text: Five infant orangutans, a species found only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra and on Borneo, were found in a forest by rangers patrolling in the Balasore district of India's eastern Odisha state last week.

Indonesia's Forestry Ministry has asked India to establish the origin of the abandoned orangutans, known for their shaggy red fur, and return them if they are found to have come from their usual habitat abroad.
The rescue of the rare apes has raised fresh questions about how exotic animals enter India and how the country is used in the illegal wildlife trade.
How did five baby orangutans end up in India?

"The discovery on the eastern coast of India is a bit mind-boggling. It's like that time a few years ago when live kangaroos were found wandering along the highways of West Bengal," said Kanitha Krishnasamy, Southeast Asia director at wildlife trade monitoring network TRAFFIC.
"What are orangutans doing in India? Were they smuggled from their native Malaysia or Indonesia or did they come from a facility?" she told DW.

blocks.caption: The youngsters appeared to be healthy and were being cared for at a zoo after their rescueImage: ANI/IMAGO

blocks.text: The Odisha government has asked the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate how the critically endangered animals reached the state.

"These animals are not found in India and are mostly seen in the rainforests of Malaysia, Indonesia, Borneo and Sumatra in Southeast Asia," said Odisha's Forest and Environment Minister Ganesh Ram Singh Khuntia.
"We suspect that they might have been released in the Balasore district forest … by an international wildlife smuggling racket."
Indian officials seize pythons, parrots, giant tortoises
The orangutans are the latest in a series of exotic wildlife being seized in India.

In November 2024, authorities in the Indian city of Bengaluru seized 40 rare animals arriving from the Malaysian capital, Kuala Lumpur, including Aldabra giant tortoises, gibbons, American alligators and iguanas.
In June 2025, Mumbai Customs seized 284 exotic animals arriving in four consignments from the Thai capital, Bangkok, including snakes and tortoises.

In July 2025, customs officials in the Indian city of Pune intercepted 20 exotic animals from passengers arriving from Bangkok. They included 14 green tree pythons, four double-eyed fig parrots and two Sumatran striped rabbits.
'Shocking' volume of trafficked wildlife found in India

According to figures from TRAFFIC network, 7,272 individual animals, alive and dead, were seized from passenger baggage in smuggling attempts between Thailand and India between January 2022 and May 2025, with more than 80% of interceptions taking place in India.
The animals included reptiles, birds and mammals — many apparently destined for the exotic pet trade.

"We have found hundreds of species and thousands of individuals being trafficked into India through air and land routes. This changed drastically from around 2020," conservation researcher and practitioner Uttara Mendiratta told DW.
"Both the volume of this trafficking, and the number of species involved, many of which are endangered, have been shocking."
Law enforcement lagging behind smugglers
TRAFFIC says India and Malaysia were the countries most implicated in an illegal gibbon trade chain identified in 2025, with gibbons being moved from Malaysia to India.
Trishala Ashok, a conservation filmmaker and science communicator, says the scale of the trade remains difficult to establish.

"Our enforcement systems haven't evolved at the same speed as the trade," Ashok told DW. "We are still reacting to individual seizures rather than mapping the networks, financiers, suppliers and buyers behind them."
Tito Joseph of the Wildlife Protection Society of India says the situation is escalating.
"Smuggling of exotic species was always there in India," Joseph told DW.
At the same time, he noted that it has increased significantly since 2018.

He identifies routes running from Myanmar through northeast India into other parts of the country, as well as movement from Bangladesh into India. By air, Thailand and Malaysia are important sources of trafficked wildlife.
The routes into India also extend beyond airports. Exotic animals are also reaching India through its northeastern land borders.

"What is new is the large volume of incoming live wildlife. There are indications that some of the traders who were involved in smuggling live animals like star tortoises out are now also involved in sourcing [other] exotic wildlife," said Mendiratta, the conservation researcher.
Social media fans illegal animal trade

Demand is being fueled by growing ownership of exotic pets and unregulated digital marketplaces, according to a June 2026 analysis of India's exotic pet trade by Humane World for Animals India, an NGO that works to tackle the root causes of animal cruelty.

"Internationally, social media platforms have aided and abetted the growth of illegal trade in wild animals by providing a platform for people to display and boast about the animals they collect," wildlife biologist and conservation scientist Ravi Chellam told DW.
"These platforms are also serving as an online marketplace for the illegal trade to flourish," he added.
"The problem is exacerbated by the senseless and obscenely huge personal collections of animals from around the world by the rich and the famous," Chellam noted.
Establishing where an animal came from can become particularly difficult once it has crossed several borders.
"A seizure cannot be the end of the investigation. It should be the beginning," said Ashok, the conservation filmmaker.

"Who supplied the animals? Who arranged the movement? Who paid? Who was waiting for them?" she asks. "Until we start following those links, we will keep catching consignments without dismantling the networks behind them."
European interest in African ants is eco-threat for everyone

articles.title: Plan to limit number of NHS patients diagnosed with ADHD attacked as ‘rationing’ healthcare
articles.summary:
Review due next week expected to say patients should be ‘triaged’ and offered support without formal diagnosis

Proposals to limit the number of patients being formally diagnosed with…
articles.byline: Anna Bawden Health and social affairs correspondent

blocks.text: Proposals to limit the number of patients being formally diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder have been atacked as “rationing” healthcare and pushing children and adults to self-diagnosis via social media.

The comments came before a government review due next week, which is expected to say that patients with ADHD symptoms should not automatically be formally diagnosed, but should be “triaged” and offered support without the need for a formal diagnosis.
Details of this “needs-based” system, first revealed in the Times, would mean NHS services target those most acutely affected by ADHD, such as those at risk of self-harm or unable to work.
Less severely affected people may not be referred for a formal diagnosis to NHS clinics but would be offered help according to a “holistic” assessment of their needs, the report will say.

The government’s independent review of mental health conditions, autism and ADHD was commissioned in December by the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, amid concerns over the sharp rise of people making sickness benefit claims due to mental health, autism and ADHD diagnoses.

Led by Prof Peter Fonagy, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst at University College London, the interim review concluded that the system forces children and adults to obtain a formal diagnosis in order to get support.

Official figures show that patients are waiting years to be assessed, with 800,000 on NHS waiting lists. Meanwhile, complaints about autism and ADHD services in England have more than tripled in five years.

As a result, growing numbers of adults and young people with ADHD are not in education, training or work, of whom about 100,000 are on health-related benefits due to their condition. The ADHD taskforce calculated that the cost of undiagnosed, untreated ADHD was £17bn.
Fonagy’s review will recommend that only patients who would benefit from a formal diagnosis, such as those needing medication, would be referred to ADHD clinics.

Under the proposed holistic needs-based assessment, patients would be triaged according to their difficulties and ability to cope at school, college, work or other settings. They would be offered targeted early support, regardless of whether they had a diagnosis or not.

Such support could include one-to-one help for children to cope with lessons, quiet rooms in schools, classes to help parents support children with ADHD symptoms, and encouraging employers to offer staff with ADHD flexible hours.
after newsletter promotion
The final report is expected to propose a similarly holistic approach to supporting people with autism, and to mental health more widely.
But experts said the proposals would in effect introduce rationing of health services and that schools and workplaces are already able to offer early support without a formal diagnosis.
Henry Shelford, the chief executive of ADHD UK, said: “This [review] proposes rationing.
“There is no ‘mild’ ADHD. Diagnosis requires evidence of a debilitating impact on your life. We already have a clinically drawn line of need.

“Without a formal diagnosis, it appears we will be left to self-diagnose via social media. Schools and businesses shouldn’t be forced to rely on TikTok to know when to put in adjustments and support.”

“On average, a woman with ADHD will die nine years younger than her peers. A man with ADHD will die seven years younger than his peers. In almost any other area, those numbers would have this treated as a health emergency, but the stigma and misunderstanding around ADHD means instead we’re treated as an inconvenience and proposed to be ‘disappeared’, untreated, from the waiting lists.

“Diagnosis means people turning their lives around, more people in employment and succeeding in careers. Investing in ADHD services has a high return on investment to the country. Last year, the NHS spent £574m on a single weight-loss drug because treating people gets them back to work. The same is true of ADHD, with cheaper medication and better evidence.”
Mel Merritt, the head of policy and influencing at the National Autistic Society, said: “Denying people a diagnosis will only worsen inequalities experienced.”

A government spokesperson would not comment on the forthcoming report, but said: “Last December, we asked clinical psychologist Prof Peter Fonagy to lead an independent review, examining the prevalence of – and support for – ADHD, autism, and mental health conditions. Prof Fonagy’s final report will be published shortly and will inform our new national approach in this area.”

articles.title: Next forecasts bigger profits after hot weather lifts sales
articles.summary: FTSE 100 retailer, which owns UK rights to US brands Gap and Victoria’s Secret, says prices could rise in autumn

blocks.text: Next has thanked warmer weather for an “unexpected” boost in sales, leading the clothing retailer to raise its profit forecasts for the fourth time this year.

The FTSE 100 company, which owns the UK rights to the US brands Gap and Victoria’s Secret as well as stakes in labels including Reiss and Joules, raised its expectations for full-year profits by £12m to £1.26bn.
It is the fourth time Next has raised profit forecasts this year, with the company having last ratcheted up its expectations in early August as Europe faced a series of heatwaves.
Next, which has more than 500 stores across the UK, said in a stock market update on Thursday: “The first half was much better than we originally anticipated, both in the UK and overseas.

“It is important to acknowledge that part of this overperformance has been the result of two unusually warm summers in the UK. The rest of the overperformance is, we believe, largely the result of fulfilling the aims we outlined at the beginning of the year.”
That has included some cost-cutting efforts, particularly across Next’s warehouses.
Overall, total sales across the group were up 9% in the six months to July, helping push pre-tax profits for the half-year up by 11% to £566m.

Next said the performance over the past six months was “all the more unexpected given the strength of sales last year”. It made £1bn of annual profits for the first time in the year ending January 2025.
However, the retailer cautioned on the impact of the rising cost of living and prospects for the jobs market.

“Our primary concerns are rising inflation, higher mortgage interest costs and a weak employment market. These worries will only be compounded if they are accompanied by tax increases,” it said, in an apparent reference to John Healey’s first budget as chancellor on 28 October.
“It seems likely that it [the government] will have to increase taxes in order to fund its expenditure.”
While the group said it was deploying AI across the business, including its tech division, Next said it was ensuring fashion designs were still led by humans.
after newsletter promotion

“In a world where AI is able to do more and more, our experience suggests that consumers prefer the authentic creativity of human beings,” it said. “That means we are putting more emphasis on designers using techniques that connect them directly to the artwork – painting, drawing, screen printing, etc. That is a big investment in time, and requires a higher level of creative talent than is needed to operate CAD [computer aided design] or prompt AI.”
Despite the strong results, the company lowered sales growth expectations in the UK, which accounts for three-quarters of total sales, from 2.8% to 2% for the six months to the end of January.

“We are looking at what’s ahead and it is sensible to moderate our expectations,” said the Next chief executive, Simon Wolfson. “We are not talking about [consumer spending] falling off a cliff. I think things are likely to get worse rather than better. Unlike in the past when the government has been able to help it doesn’t have any room for manoeuvre. It has a £100bn deficit. That means not only can we not expect the government to necessarily alleviate the problem, but potentially make it worse.”
He added that the escalation of hostilities in the Middle East has not triggered a further increase in further potential cost increases for Next.

“We are not expecting shipping costs to get higher, there is already a surcharge we are paying,” Wolfson said. “All those cost increases are baked in [since the start of the conflict in February], and if anything are not as bad as March.”

Aarin Chiekrie, an equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, said: “Next delivered its first-half results in style, with sales growth accelerating over the period and breezing past the fashion company’s original guidance. In the UK, hotter-than-expected weather and more effective marketing saw customers logging in to refresh their summer wardrobes online, helping offset a small decline in-store.”

articles.title: PH still deadliest country in Asia for environmental defenders for 13th straight year
articles.summary: The latest report from watchdog group Global Witness says violence against defenders in the Philippines in 2025 was linked to the government's counterinsurgency programs and extractive projects

blocks.text: PROTEST. Community and church partners of EcoWaste Coalition reenact the Way of the Cross along the streets of Tondo, Manila, on March 31, 2026, to call for just and lasting solutions to the nation’s worsening waste, climate, energy, and corruption issues.
Rappler
The latest report from watchdog group Global Witness says violence against defenders in the Philippines in 2025 was linked to the government's counterinsurgency programs and extractive projects

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines recorded 12 killings of land and environmental defenders in 2025, the highest in Asia, according to a report by watchdog group Global Witness released on Wednesday, September 16.
This is the 13th consecutive time the Philippines ranked as the deadliest country for environmental defenders in Asia.
These are the environmental defenders identified by Global Witness in its 2025 report:

items: Ali Jejhon Macalintal
Davie Ugking
Fernando Promboy
Hulyo Agtay
Joan Escuadro
Juan Sumilhig
Nickasio Tayas Mindo
Ramon Lupos
Rico Malubay
Rudolph Dela Cruz Espe
Veronico Anterio
Warlita Jimenez

blocks.text: Global Witness said violence against defenders in the Philippines was linked to the government’s counterinsurgency programs and extractive projects. Five of the killings involved the suspected participation of members of the Philippine military, according to the report.
Kalikasan People’s Network for the Environment, in a statement on Thursday, September 17, condemened the attacks against environmental defenders.
“The right to defend the land is the right to defend life. The right to protest is a fundamental right, never a crime,” the group said.

Kalikasan also accused state institutions, including security and legal agencies, of being used to target communities through what it described as fabricated charges, terrorist accusations, and intimidation.

Last September 10, five paralegals were arrested, while dozens were hurt in a protest against Pax Silica. The protest was held outside an event where President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. was meeting investors for the Luzon development project.
Environmental groups have raised concerns over the environmental impacts of Pax Silica in the country.

The Global Witness report said at least 124 land and environmental defenders were killed globally in 2025, with Colombia remaining the deadliest country with 39 cases, followed by Brazil with 26 cases. The Philippines tied with Honduras at third with 12 cases. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Nicholas Brandram’s family deny he was ‘Putney pusher’ and say Met police pressure led to his death
articles.summary:
Banker, 44, was arrested in connection with 2017 incident but family say ‘no credible evidence’ he was involved

The family of Nicholas Brandram have denied he was the so-called “Putney…

blocks.text: The family of Nicholas Brandram have denied he was the so-called “Putney pusher” and said he “took his own life after months of immense pressure caused by a Metropolitan police investigation”.
Brandram, 44, was found unresponsive inside a property in Chiswick, west London, believed to be his home, on Tuesday evening.
The senior city banker had been arrested in June in connection with an incident nearly 10 years ago on Putney Bridge, in which a jogger shoved a woman headfirst into the path of an oncoming bus.
The Metropolitan police said Brandram had been released under investigation after his arrest.

A statement released on behalf of his immediate family on Thursday said Brandram had taken his own life after “months of immense pressure caused by a Metropolitan police investigation into whether he was the so-called ‘Putney Pusher’”.
His family denied his involvement in the incident and claimed the police had no forensic evidence linking him to it.

They said: “There was no forensic evidence linking Nick to it, no evidence placing him on Putney Bridge at that time, and no credible evidence that he was the man shown in the footage. In fact, the evidence proved the opposite.

“Despite that, the police chose to arrest Nick rather than invite him to attend for interview. They searched his home, and the Met police press team then released information which inevitably led to speculation and Nick being identified in subsequent reporting.”

The family added: “For Nick, the consequences did not disappear. He was left for months carrying the stigma of an appalling allegation which the police themselves clearly recognised was unsupported by the evidence.
“He lived with the shame, anxiety, humiliation, and extraordinary pressure created by a wholly unnecessary investigation.”

They said the police had repeatedly been asked to end their investigation and had been warned about the impact the investigation was having on Brandram’s mental health, saying: “Even then, the investigation was not brought to an end. As a result, Nick is dead.”
The Met have been approached for comment.
Brandram was a director at HSBC and had previously served in the military, reaching the rank of captain.

He was the grandson of Princess Katherine of Greece, who was the great-granddaughter of Queen Victoria, the Daily Telegraph reported in 2013, when he was convicted of crashing his Harley-Davidson motorbike into a female cyclist around Hyde Park Corner and driving off without leaving his details.
In an interview with the Citywealth website in March this year, Brandram said he was a senior relationship manager at HSBC Private Bank.

He said: “I usually bicycle into our office in Mayfair from my home in west London. And then from there, can either stay at my desk, go to Canary Wharf or the City, or get on a train or go to the airport. My first meeting is ideally over breakfast and I’m ideally home for bath time. I’m a co-parenting single father with a three-year-old.”

Brandram said his proudest professional achievement was being invited to a Buckingham Palace garden party after military service in Afghanistan, and that the person he most admired was his mother. “She raised three children as a single parent and is the busiest person I know,” he said. “I’ve never met someone with greater moral integrity and courage, as well as resilience and stamina.”

articles.title: Fact check: How disinformation fuels Houthi-Saudi conflict
articles.summary: As fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia escalates this month, old and repurposed videos have flooded social media, with many presented as fresh footage from the front line.

image.caption: This satellite image shows a pumping station along the general route of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline following an attack by Yemen's Iran-backed HouthisImage: Vantor/AFP

blocks.text: The conflict between Yemen's Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia has sharply escalated in recent days, with Houthi forces making rapid gains along the Red Sea coast and taking control of key areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Saudi Arabia has responded with airstrikes, while Houthi forces have launched drones and missiles towards Saudi territory. The renewed fighting has also raised concerns about global trade through the Red Sea.
The conflict has also spread online, where significant disinformation has circulated.
DW's fact-checking team examined what is circulating and why a conflict that is so hard to observe independently leaves so much room for this kind of disinformation.
Nine-second clip getting viral
One nine-second clip has gone viral. It shows a huge explosion between buildings, with fireballs and screaming in the background.

Claim: A user posted the video on X with the Arabic caption, "Yemeni forces are carrying out the strongest strikes in various areas in Saudi Arabia, including Abha." The video has more than 340,000 views.
It was also posted in other languages, falsely claiming it showed real footage from the current fighting.

blocks.caption: Towards the end of the clip, a lamp post emerges out of nowhere, a clear sign that the video was AI-generatedImage: X

blocks.text: DW Fact check: Fake and AI-generated
The video is not only old, but also artificially generated. There are several visual clues in the clip: the pattern of the explosions and the uniform way the smoke spreads.

A large-scale explosion of this kind would also have generated a very bright flash, and nearby buildings would likely have collapsed or at least had their windows shattered. Neither appears to have happened.
One can also see, in the final seconds of the video, how a lamppost appears out of nowhere in the middle of the frame.

The audio is mostly unintelligible, but the speaker's tone does not appear to change after the huge explosion. Such a large explosion would normally be expected to trigger some audible reaction in the speaker's voice.
On the technical side, Hive Moderation's AI detection analysis also confirmed that the video was artificially generated.

blocks.caption: According to AI detection platform Hive Moderation, there are clear indications that the video was generated using artificial intelligenceImage: Hive Moderation

blocks.text: And this is not the first time this video has been posted. The very same video was shared this June, claiming to show explosions in Iran, as we found with a reverse image search.
Not enough verified information from Yemen
The recycling of old or unrelated footage is not new to the Yemen conflict.
Hannah Porter has spent years researching fake news and disinformation in Yemen and the country's wider information environment. She says this has been happening for years.

"There is less international attention in Yemen than there might be in other conflicts around the world. And because there is not sufficient attention paid to Yemen, I think that allows more space for disinformation to spread not only within Yemen and in the region, but globally about Yemen," Porter said in an interview with DW.
The Houthis seized Yemini capital Sanaa and expanded their control in 2014. Saudi Arabia intervened militarily in 2015 in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.
A UN-brokered truce in 2022 sharply reduced fighting, but it did not resolve the conflict. Fighting has since intensified again.
The Houthis now control large parts of northern and western Yemen. Saudi Arabia supports forces opposing them, while Iran has provided the Houthis with military support.

Experts and media watchdogs like Reporters Without Borders have repeatedly pointed out that reporting from some parts of Yemen remains extremely difficult. Journalists face threats, while independent media outlets are under intense pressure. This contributes to the spread of disinformation.
It is "very difficult to get reliable information, especially now and especially in the North [of Yemen]," Porter said.
She said researchers and the international community are also struggling to establish what is happening in northern Yemen.
Military exercise becomes ambush
The second video that DW Fact check examined shows how genuine footage can become a source of disinformation.

Claim: A 30-second clip posted on X shows a convoy of military vehicles passing through a desert. Moments later, large explosions erupt and several vehicles are engulfed in smoke and flames. The caption reads: "The most beautiful thing I've seen: Houthis ambush against the Saudi-Backed Mercenaries' convoy in Yemeni."

blocks.caption: This video does not show an ambush by the Houthis, a Yemeni rebel groupImage: X

blocks.text: DW Fact check: False
The video is old and unrelated to the ongoing conflict.
A timestamp visible in the video points to March 10, 2024. A reverse image search led DW to an older video published on YouTube in April 2024.

That video claims to show a Houthi military exercise. Its caption, written in Arabic, describes a simulated ambush on Israeli positions and attacks on US and British forces. Israeli and American flags can be seen in the footage.
DW also traced the sequence to a 42-minute video published by Yemeni War Media, an outlet affiliated with the Houthi movement.

Interestingly, the audio of that clip was changed. The version that is now circulating contains dramatic commentary, which is actually sports commentary from a football match played in 2018, as clips from that match show.
As is often the case, the clip with the convoy has also been used previously in different contexts.
Houthi gains in Yemen threaten key Red Sea shipping route
With much of Yemen's media landscape weakened by the conflict, reliable information about events can be difficult to obtain.

That makes it harder for people to independently assess footage circulating online, Porter says, adding that such unverified or misattributed videos can significantly shape perceptions of how battles are unfolding elsewhere.
"Any image or video that you see that is purported to be of a specific battle in Yemen, you have to be really skeptical and you have to find a way to fact check it."
Emad Hassan contributed to this article
Edited by Uta Steinwehr and Thomas Sparrow

articles.title: ICE agent arrested in Minneapolis on charges of assault and false reporting of crime
articles.summary:
Christian Castro faced assault charges after shooting Venezuelan man through the door of his apartment while children were present

A federal immigration officer wanted on assault charges for…

blocks.text: A federal immigration officer wanted on assault charges for shooting and ​wounding a Venezuelan man in Minneapolis was arrested there on Wednesday, eight months after a confrontation that became a flashpoint over ‌Donald Trump’s deportation sweeps.

Christian Castro, an Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent, was taken into custody by agents of the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension in Minneapolis and was booked into the Hennepin county jail on his outstanding arrest warrant, the agency said.

Castro had been released on bond from federal custody earlier this month, after an initial appearance in a district court ​in McAllen, Texas, on charges of lying to investigators about the circumstances of the 14 January shooting.

Under an agreement with Minnesota law enforcement, ​Castro voluntarily drove to Minneapolis from Texas to turn himself in to state authorities at his attorney’s office but ended ⁠up being arrested minutes before he was due to arrive, the lawyer, Daniel Gerdts, told Reuters.

Another lawyer representing the ICE agent, Rolando Cantu, said his ​client always had intended to answer to the charges in Minneapolis. He disputed Hennepin county prosecutors’ assertions that Castro might flee to Mexico, saying: “He wants his ​day in court.”

The federal indictment charging Castro with making false statements marked the first justice department prosecution of a federal law enforcement officer accused of wrongdoing arising from the massive Minneapolis ICE deployment dubbed Operation Metro Surge.
That operation, part of Trump’s wider immigration crackdown, drew weeks of protests and clashes between ICE and demonstrators, leading to ​the fatal shootings of two US citizens by federal agents.

Castro already faced state assault charges in Minnesota stemming from the confrontation in which he shot Julio ​Cesar Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan national, in the leg through the door of the man’s apartment while children were present inside the home.

The state charges also include false reporting of ‌a crime ⁠after Castro allegedly told superiors at the Department of Homeland Security that Sosa-Celis and others attacked him with a snow shovel and broom, which was disproved by video evidence.
Initial efforts to arrest Castro were thwarted when the ICE agent returned to his home state of Texas, leading Minnesota officials to issue a warrant for his arrest.

Castro was apprehended by Texas Rangers, but Greg Abbott, a Republican and supporter of Trump’s mass deportation sweeps, refused to sign ​extradition papers sent by Tim ​Walz, Minnesota’s democratic governor.

Abbott questioned whether ⁠Castro could be considered a fugitive from justice, and thus subject to extradition, because DHS had reassigned him to his home state of Texas after the Minneapolis shooting.

The ICE agent ultimately spent 90 days in a Texas county jail and ​was released on 27 August after a federal judge in Texas denied a request from Minnesota to immediately ​order his extradition. Castro ⁠was re-arrested in Texas after his federal grand jury indictment in early September.
DHS has suspended Castro from ICE, and a person familiar with the case has said a civil rights investigation into the Sosa-Celis shooting had been opened.

Castro was expected to make his first state court appearance in Minneapolis on Thursday. He will then make ⁠an initial appearance ​in a District Court in neighboring St Paul, the state capital, on Friday morning to ​face charges in the federal indictment.

“Governor Abbott’s attempt to shield Mr Castro from accountability has failed. We look forward to commencing our prosecution,” said Mary Moriarty, the Hennepin county attorney who brought the state ​case, in a statement.

articles.title: South Africa: Police find 9th body of woman amid spree fears
articles.summary: Police in South Africa have discovered the bodies of nine women east of Johannesburg in two months, stoking fears of a serial killer or group of killers.

image.caption: Police are probing whether the latest find is tied to a series of recent femicidesImage: Emmanuel Croset/AFP

blocks.text: Police in South Africa on Thursday found the body of another woman near the airport east of Johannesburg.
The woman's body was found stabbed, beaten and partially naked.
The body is the ninth that has been discovered in the area in the last two months, raising fears that the killings could be connected and that a serial killer — or group of killers — might be active.
What do we know about the latest discovery of a woman's body near Johannesburg?
The bobies were all discovered in Ekurhuleni, a municipality immediately east of Johannesburg, the country's largest city.
Both Ekurhuleni and Johannesburg lie in Gauteng province.
Fred Kekana, the provincial police commissioner, said the woman's body was found near a construction site by a passerby, who alerted police.

The victim, who has not been identified, appeared to be around 30 years old and had a stab wound to her side. Her throat also appeared to have been cut, Kekana said, although the cause of death has not yet been officially determined.
Previously, investigators had said similarities in the killings of the first eight victims were "sufficiently concerning for the police to issue a public warning."
Police said the latest find early Thursday would be "added to the investigations into the deaths of women in Ekurhuleni."
A lockdown has been put in place in Kempton Park in Ekurhuleni and police have set up roadblocks, after three of the bodies were discovered in recent days.
"We cannot continue picking up bodies," deputy police chief Tebello Mosikili told journalists at the scene on Thursday.

blocks.caption: Residents of the area have been left shaken by the killingsImage: Emmanuel Croset/AFP

blocks.text: Killings send shockwaves through South Africa
Mosikili said investigators look at whether the latest find is linked to the earlier murders or if a so-called copycat killer is also active.
Police have offered a reward of 400,000 rand (about $25,000 or €21,400) for information leading to an arrest.
The premier of Gauteng province, Panyaza Lesufi, said Thursday that "someone has declared war against us, and we will push back, we are not going to surrender."
President Cyril Ramaphosa said Tuesday that "no stone will be left unturned" to solve the crimes.
"These incidents are causing fear and uncertainty in our communities, and especially among women," Ramaphosa said.
South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world, and gender-based violence is also endemic. The country has declared a national emergency to tackle the issue.
The UN estimates that one in three women experiences physical or sexual violence during her lifetime.

articles.title: Europe seeks stricter age limits for TikTok, Instagram and Facebook
articles.summary: The European Commission wants to bar children under 13 from social media platforms and curb addictive features such as infinite scrolling. Companies that fail to comply could face hefty fines.

image.caption: Von der Leyen is pushing for new rules to keep children off social mediaImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, unveiled a plan aimed at keeping children away from the risks associated with some social media platforms.
The initiative seeks to prevent children under the age of 13 from accessing platforms such as Facebook, TikTok, and Instagram.
"What we already have is a consensus that there needs to be a start date for the age children can join social media," von der Leyen said, calling for "age-appropriate restrictions."

The measure follows similar proposals introduced in Australia, the United Kingdom, China, India, Turkey, and several European countries, and responds to growing concerns about the impact social media can have on children's mental health.

"Today, our children are interacting with some of the most sophisticated technologies ever created, and they were not designed with their well-being and development in mind," von der Leyen said at a press conference.
The proposed reform to the EU Kids Act "will establish clear boundaries in the digital world, just as we do every day in the real world," she added.
Do European laws contradict each other?

The non-profit organization CCIA Europe, which represents major technology companies in Europe, including Google and Meta, warned about potential privacy risks stemming from the proposal and pointed to "conflicting requirements" under other European Union laws.

"Collecting age information, identity credentials, and data linking children to their parents or guardians on this scale would undoubtedly create an attractive target for cybercriminals," said CCIA Europe Director Daniel Friedlaender.
"The Kids Act creates legal overlap and regulatory duplication that ultimately weakens protections for children and consumers," he added.
Can AI tell if you're 18+ just from your hand movements?
More parental control and stricter regulations
Von der Leyen's proposal would give parents greater control over the accounts of young people aged 13 to 15.
The initiative will be debated among EU member states and the European Parliament in the coming months before it can become law.
Social media accounts, video streaming services, online video games, and chatbots aimed at users under 18 would be subject to a set of stricter regulations.

These include banning features considered addictive, such as infinite scrolling and autoplay content. The proposal would also restrict algorithm-driven recommendations, personalized profiling, reward-based engagement mechanisms, and unsolicited contact from strangers.
Another demand from the European Parliament is that platforms be required to implement child-safe designs and algorithms, while also providing easy-to-use parental controls.
In addition, major technology companies would have to strengthen their age-verification systems for anyone seeking to open an account.
Companies that fail to comply could face fines of up to 6% of their global annual revenue.
They would also be required to dedicate greater resources to content supervision and moderation.

articles.title: Swedish PM Kristersson resigns after election loss
articles.summary: Left-wing opposition parties led by Magdalena Andersson look set to form the next government.

blocks.text: Sweden's Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has resigned after his ruling right-wing bloc was narrowly defeated by the centre-left opposition in the country's general election.

He made the announcement in a post on X on Thursday afternoon, after preliminary votes from Sunday's election showed about 50,000 votes separated the two blocs in the country of about 10 million people.
Opposition parties led by Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats look set to win 176 seats in the 349-seat Riksdag, Sweden's parliament.
Kristersson, a conservative, had been supported in government by the anti-immigration hard-right Sweden Democrats (SD), and had promised them cabinet jobs if he won the election.
His right-wing bloc looks set to win 173 seats in the Riksdag, according to data from the Swedish Election Authority.
The results will be subject to formal certification in the coming days and are expected to finalised this weekend.
In Sweden, there are two major political blocs - with four parties on the right and four on the left, so Swedes are used to coalition and minority governments.
After a prime minister resigns, the Speaker of the Riksdag holds talks with all parties to proposes a candidate for the next leader, which is then voted on by MPs.

"Now it is the speaker who will lead the next stage of the way to a new government. I am herewith requesting that I be relieved of the office of prime minister to allow that work to start immediately," Kristersson's statement read.
Andersson has initiated talks with the other opposition parties - The Left Party, The Centre Party and The Green Party - about forming a government.
But discussions could drag on due to major differences between the parties on issues such as taxes.
After the 2022 election in Sweden, it took 37 days to form a government, while in 2018 it took 134 days.
In his resignation, Kristersson said the opposition faced "complicated" conditions for forming the next government, "because the parties' various statements before election day could pose obstacles".
The right-wing bloc is formed of Kristersson's Moderates, as well as the SD, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals.
The SD were founded by Nazi sympathisers in the 1980s and were shunned for decades by the mainstream.

But the party has rebranded itself since the mid-2000s, culminating in a watershed moment in 2022 when it became Sweden's second-largest party on a campaign focused on issues around immigration and violent crime.

They had offered outside support to the current centre-right coalition, which had overseen a dramatic tightening of migration policy. Kristersson had promised to bring them into government if he remained at the helm.
But in a surprise upset for the party, it lost support for the first time since entering parliament in 2010 - down three percentage points on 2022.
A preliminary vote count started after voting closed on Sunday evening and continued into this week.
On Wednesday, election committees began counting early votes that were submitted late, as well as votes from abroad that did not arrive before election day.

blocks.text: The Albanese government is considering a “world-leading” ban on smart glasses in its offices and service centres as councils around Australia push the technology out of public spaces over privacy fears.
The government has avoided a sweeping ban on the import of the camera-equipped technology and encouraged individual workplaces to set their own rules.
The public service minister, Katy Gallagher, said on Thursday she had asked the Australian public service for advice on whether the glasses should be prohibited.
“We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Gallagher said.
“Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information.”
Commonwealth-run workplaces range from bureaucrats’ offices to Centrelink service centres and CSIRO laboratories.
Schools and hospitals run by state governments would be left to set their own rules over the technology, which have grown increasingly popular but raised public outcry.
A University of Sydney study of smart glasses-filmed videos posted on Instagram found 60% of a sample could be classified as potential harassment.
The Albanese government said it was seeking to set a world-leading standard. So far, no national government has banned the glasses’ use across their agencies.

Courts in England and Wales in the UK and New York state in the US have banned the technology, while the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency reportedly classified them as body-worn cameras and barred them from the “federal workspace”.

A local council in Sydney on Tuesday became the latest to issue a targeted bans on the use of the technology. Canterbury-Bankstown’s mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called “pervert glasses” as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools.
In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools and Melbourne’s Yarra city council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms.
The City of Sydney and the Blacktown city councils have prohibited pool patrons from using smart glasses to record.
Speaking to Channel Seven earlier this month, the federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, praised councils’ decisions and said she would consult businesses on their approach.
“Businesses know that good privacy is good business,” Rowland said.
“But … we want to make sure we get the balance right and we don’t unfairly discriminate against people who are using this technology to better participate in society.”

Vision Australia and some people living with disabilities have praised the technology as a support for people who are blind or have low vision. Rowland said the government was not pursuing a ban but had not “ruled anything out”.
Gallagher said she wanted the Australian public service to set the national standard as a “model employer”.
“Technology is changing rapidly and as a major employer the Commonwealth needs to make sure our workplace policies keep pace,” Gallagher said.
Pending restrictions on smart glasses would be the federal government’s latest workplace technology reform after it issued guidance on the use of AI in the public service last week.
The guidelines indicate employees would not need to be consulted on every new tool but should be consulted for major initiatives or changes to how they carry out work.

Major businesses will contribute to new national guidelines on AI in workplaces, with Commonwealth Bank, Microsoft, AGL, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and Ramsay Health Care to attend a roundtable on Friday.
Amanda Rishworth, the employment minister, said the government wanted to use the roundtable to take on the lessons of businesses already using AI.
“Workers and businesses need the capability to adopt new technologies with confidence that appropriate safeguards are in place,” Rishworth said.
Additional reporting from Caitlin Cassidy

articles.title: Burnham has to sell Bank rate rises as ‘breathing space’ – good luck with that
articles.summary: PM’s push to cut cost of living is threatened by rising inflation and higher government borrowing costs

blocks.text: Good luck to Andy Burnham convincing voters he is giving them “breathing space,” if the Bank of England ratchets up interest rates in the coming months.

That was the prospect opened up by Thursday’s minutes of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) meeting, which left rates unchanged at 3.75% – for now – but suggested policymakers may be unlikely to hold out much longer.
“If the conflict in the Middle East persists for an extended period, as appears to be the case,” the Bank governor, Andrew Bailey warned. “It is likely that policy may have to tighten.”
With classic Bank understatement, Bailey warned that since hostilities heated up again, there had been, “a seeming loss of urgency to find solutions”.
When the new prime minister arrived in Downing Street in July, the war had abated, and the UK economy was puttering along nicely.
Since then, the resumption of the Iran conflict has pushed global oil prices back above $100 a barrel, with painful knock-on effects across Europe and Asia.

In the UK, inflation hit 3.1% in August, driven by rising fuel prices. And even without a rate rise from the Bank, mortgage rates have already jumped, as markets contemplate a period of higher inflation. The MPC now expects inflation to be above 4% in the first quarter of 2027.

The minutes of the their meeting suggested a marked reluctance to raise rates for now. While energy prices have shot up, the jobs market remains weak, helping to contain the risks of the “second-round effects” that allow inflation to become embedded.

And the six:three vote for a hold was the same as at their last meeting in July, suggesting no rush to jump immediately. Yet there was also a growing sense of concern about the impact of soaring energy costs.
The widely expected hold decision leaves the Bank an outlier among leading central banks.

Kevin Warsh, chair of the US Federal Reserve, defied Trump’s urgent calls for rate cuts on Wednesday by increasing US borrowing costs for the first time since 2023 – a move that went down well in financial markets, but predictably infuriated the president. The ECB raised rates last week; the Bank of Japan is expected to follow on Friday.
after newsletter promotion
Burnham kicked off his premiership with modest but tangible cost of living measures, such as capping bus fares and slashing VAT on electricity bills.

But he now faces a double whammy. Higher inflation and energy prices threaten to overwhelm the benefits of such handouts; but higher interest rates on government borrowing has increased the costs of future measures to protect consumers.
All this at a time when – as the MPC acknowledges – weather shocks are likely to push up food prices, and bond markets remain fragile.
The new prime minister has made clear that he expects to focus more on domestic affairs and less on striding the global stage than his beleaguered predecessor Keir Starmer.
But if – as currently seems likely – the Iran war goes on and on, the costs of global geopolitics will be felt at home regardless.

articles.title: Klopp wants Germany football team to 'reclaim the flag'
articles.summary: Jürgen Klopp says he wants his Germany team to reclaim pride in being German after recent political developments.

image.caption: Jürgen Klopp engaged with a number of topics at his squad announcement press conference, and was not afraid to discuss politicsImage: Hannes P. Albert/AFP

blocks.text: Jürgen Klopp used his first squad announcement as Germany's new head coach to deliver a stirring speech in favor of what he described as "positive patriotism."
"I'd like to reclaim the flag for myself—or for us," Klopp said.

"I want us to always wave it in a way that makes no one think, 'What's wrong with you?' But rather, that people simply get the feeling that you're happy and understand how lucky you are to have been born, raised, or moved to this wonderful country."
This was an apparent reference to the recent state election in Saxony-Anhalt, which the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) won.
Klopp said of the election "that some people probably thought it was okay, while many others thought: 'Good heavens, what's going on there?"

The former Borussia Dortmund and Liverpool head coach was quick to say he is not a political expert and that he doesn't want to talk about politics at every press conference, but that he doesn't want to "leave national pride to the wrong people."
Rather than leaving that up to misinterpretation though, something Klopp said was possible, he turned towards the concept of "positive patriotism."
"I can be proud to be German and still be open-minded, diverse, kind, and friendly," he said. "I actually think we're a wonderful country."

The 59-year-old added that just as he had selected the current squad by looking at what the country had to offer in terms of football talent rather than what it was lacking, it might help to do the same when looking at the country as a whole.
This echoed a similar sentiment of former Germany head coach Julian Nagelsmann, who spoke emotionally after Germany's Euro 2024 exit.
"Being together must become more important again. We must not be consumed with envy, always paint everything in a negative light and not begrudge our neighbors anything," Nagelsmann said.
"If everyone in their small circle, on their street, starts to help and support their neighbors, not always seeing the negative, integrating people. That is important."
Klopp highlights the power of football
Klopp was quick to turn to the power of football, while also recognizing its place in wider society.

"It's more important that we have doctors. It's more important that we have nurses. It's more important that we have a great, great many people in a wide variety of professions," he said, before adding that football can "foster a sense of community that lets us truly feel the power of sports."

Klopp cited the recent successes of Alexander Zverev, the world champion field hockey team, the home World Cup in women's basketball, and the success of athletes at this summer's European Athletics Championships as further positive examples of the power of sport.
"That's our mission. We have to create the right atmosphere—I know that. But to do that, we need people who are willing to embrace it," he said.

blocks.caption: "One of 83 million" was the message on Jürgen Klopp's hatImage: Hannes P. Albert/AFP

blocks.text: A masterclass in communication

Klopp's delivery was a textbook example of how to create alignment across his messaging. His squad, made up of 44 players including 11 new faces, is a reflection of the diverse society that Klopp referenced he was proud of.

His engagement with the media was also strategically smart. After laying down clear boundaries in his first press conference that included him saying he would quit if coverage strayed into the personal, Klopp this time opted to seek to include the media as part of the process while also subtly reminding them of what he sees as their role.

When explaining his choice to name such a large squad with so many new and young players, Klopp said he wasn't going to tell members of the media how to do their job when it comes to assessing players but said that he knew how he would do it. In between the lines, this was an indirect appeal to the media to choose coverage that would foster the development of this new era of players rather than hinder it by being overly critical or negative.

On top of that, he did all of this while wearing a baseball cap with the words "one of 83 million" written on the front. This is in reference to a Germany's approximate population and an expression about how everyone has an opinion on the Germany team and so is therefore a "Bundestrainer" (national team coach). It also came across as an attempt to make everyone responsible for the success of this team.

Germany's Euro 2024 campaign briefly instilled some pride over the flag again, as did Germany's women in the Euro 2022 final. The most impactful though, was the 2006 World Cup in Germany, which provided the biggest positive cultural shift in the general German attitude towards national pride since World War II.

Now, through the vehicle of football, Germany's new head coach has declared a desire to restore that pride. Klopp said his whole career had brought him to this moment. After these words, it felt like all the disappointments the Germany team – and fans have endured over the last few years may just have brought them to the right leader too.

articles.title: UN mission finds grounds to believe U.S. committed war crimes in strikes on Iranian school, sports centre
articles.summary: A United Nations fact-finding mission on Iran said on Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school ‌and sports facility in Iran in…

image.caption: A child runs past a banner strung across the rubble of the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, Iran, showing portraits of the children and teachers killed there by a Feb. 28 U.S. airstrike. (Vahid Salemi/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

A United Nations fact-finding mission on Iran said on Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school ‌and sports facility in Iran in February, and that these constituted war crimes.
United Nations experts highlight indiscriminate strikes on school in Minab, sports centre in Lamerd

A United Nations fact-finding mission on Iran said Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school ‌and sports facility in Iran in February, and that these constituted war crimes.

It also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests that occurred just weeks before the U.S. and Israel launched airstrikes on Iran on Feb. 28.

The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined the American conduct during the Iran war that began in February and ​the Iranian government's response to nationwide unrest that began in late December.
The Iranian and U.S. ​permanent missions in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
U.S. officials have previously said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.
Dozens of schoolchildren killed

The ​UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe U.S. forces were responsible for an attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh ⁠Primary School in Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according ‌to Iranian officials.
The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.
U.S. responsible for strike on Iran school, internal military probe reportedly finds

According to the report, the U.S. relied on intelligence suggesting a senior Iranian military commander was present at the site but failed to adequately verify the information before launching the strike. Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence ⁠and confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.

"Rather, the U.S. directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen."

items: Video appears to contradict Trump claim that U.S. wasn't responsible for deadly Minab school blast
Several U.S. military bases, diplomatic buildings have been damaged in Iran war: inspector general report

blocks.text: Reuters first reported that an initial internal U.S. military investigation showed U.S. forces were likely responsible for the fatal strike in Minab.
The Pentagon has since elevated the probe but it has not published any preliminary findings. U.S. President Donald Trump initially blamed Iran for the attack.
UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found ​no evidence that it was being used for military purposes.

The experts reached a similar conclusion over a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd, Iran. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and ⁠a school, and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
U.S. Central Command said in ⁠a statement in March that American forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.
Iran's biggest crackdown in decades condemned

The UN mission ⁠probe found ⁠that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic ​attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.

Rights groups ​say bystanders were among those killed ⁠during the biggest crackdown since Shia Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled opponents and foreign foes, including the U.S. and Israel.
Reporting from inside Iran

The probe said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was likely far higher than official figures which say 3,038 people were killed and 25,000 people were injured.

The government's response to the protests — including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of ⁠the death penalty — marked a significant escalation from ‌previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

articles.title: Serbia's President Vucic criticizes Kosovo war crimes verdict
articles.summary: The conviction of four former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders has drawn sharply different reactions across the Balkans. Serbia has accused the court of failing to fully address crimes against Serbs.

image.caption: Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci (pictured here in court in The Hague in 2023) was sentenced to 25 years in prison on WednesdayImage: Koen van Weel/ANP/AFP

blocks.text: The Kosovo war crimes tribunal in The Hague on Wednesday found four former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) guilty of war crimes committed during the 1998–99 Kosovo war.

The war was fought between the forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia, on the one side, and the KLA on the other, and took place in the context of the breakup of the former Yugoslavia.

Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci and former KLA leaders Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi were sentenced at first instance by the Kosovo Specialist Chambers to a combined 81 years in prison: Thaci and Krasniqi to 25 years each, Veseli to 18 and Selimi to 13 years.
The four men were convicted of the arbitrary detention of 385 people, cruel treatment of 49 people, torture of 303 people and the murder of 96 people.
They were acquitted of the charges of crimes against humanity on the grounds that it had not been proven that there had been a widespread or systematic attack directed against a civilian population.
Vucic: Court 'did not want to undermine KLA's credibility'

Speaking at a press conference on Wednesday evening, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic criticized the fact that the Kosovo Specialist Chambers (which is part of Kosovo's judicial system but is based in The Hague and staffed by international judges) did not convict the four former KLA leaders of crimes against humanity.

blocks.caption: Vucic criticized the ruling by the Kosovo Specialist Chambers on WednesdayImage: Filip Stevanovic/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: "As a court of the so-called Kosovo, they did not want to undermine the credibility of the KLA and did not address the merits of the matter concerning the formation of forces aimed at seceding Kosovo from Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia," he said.

Vucic added that the verdict did not cover crimes committed against Serbs after June 20, 1999, when KFOR, an international peacekeeping mission led by NATO, arrived in Kosovo after the armed conflict had officially ended.
'United in hatred against Serbs'
Vucic had strong words on the reactions to the verdict from several states of the former Yugoslavia.

Commenting on Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti's assessment that the verdict represented an "unacceptable injustice," Vucic said: "Imagine if we had said that about any defendant or convicted person. How many resolutions and declarations would various European and world parliaments have adopted against our people and our country?"

This was an allusion to the condemnation by European officials of the funeral last week of former Bosnian Serb commander and convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, which was attended by large numbers of citizens and several Serbian government ministers in Belgrade.
Hague tribunal convicts Hashim Thaci of Kosovo war crimes

Vucic also commented on a statement issued by Croatia's Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs, which said the verdict did not change the fact that the people of Kosovo had been victims of repression and crimes committed by Serbian leader Slobodan Milosevic's regime.
"There are no Serbs as victims; in every statement, Serbs have to be the perpetrators," said Vucic. "All of them in the region are united in hatred against Serbs."
Individualization of criminal responsibility
Serbian lawyer Aleksandar Olenik, who works on war crimes cases in the former Yugoslavia, gave a positive assessment of the ruling.

"It is well known that war crimes were committed in the territory of Kosovo that was under the control of the KLA during the 1990s. We now have judgments and the individualization of criminal responsibility," he told DW.

blocks.caption: Serbian lawyer Aleksandar Olenik said that the respect shown for victims in the proceedings in The Hague represents 'progress in international criminal law'Image: Media Center in Belgrade

blocks.text: Olenik pointed out that the respect shown for victims in the proceedings in The Hague represents "progress in international criminal law."
"In previous ad hoc tribunals, victims were merely witnesses, merely a means of proving guilt. At this court, they have their own legal representative and are entitled to compensation," he said.
More trials to come in Kosovo?
Olenik explained that in accordance with the Kosovo law that established the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, only the founders of the KLA are subject to prosecution before that court.
Kosovo's domestic judiciary will prosecute other members of the organization believed to have committed crimes.

blocks.caption: There was shock and disbelief in Kosovo after the verdict was announcedImage: Ermal Meta/Matrix Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: "The summary of the judgment names individuals who were not included in the indictment but who were found to have committed criminal offenses," he said. "It is now up to the other part of Kosovo's judicial system to prosecute, first, those against whom evidence was presented in these proceedings, and then others as well. This should also cover the period after the end of the armed conflict, that is, after June 20, 1999."
Serbia, Kosovo 'heighten the potential for conflict'

Stasa Zajovic of Women in Black, a Belgrade-based NGO founded in the early 1990s that is primarily engaged in anti-war activities, said neither the "Serbian regime nor the Kosovo authorities" use judgments in war crimes cases "to examine their own responsibility in the war, but rather to heighten the potential for conflict."

"When I say that they use similar patterns, I cannot equate the scale of the crimes committed by the two sides. It must not be forgotten that the Serbian regime is responsible for the largest number of atrocities in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, particularly in Kosovo," she told DW.
Speaking about tensions in Kosovo following the pronouncement of the verdict in The Hague on Wednesday, Zajovic said "it is important that international forces are present to monitor the situation."

blocks.caption: Disbelief soon turned to anger in Pristina as protesters clashed with riot police outside the headquarters of the European Union Rule of Law Mission in KosovoImage: Valdrin Xhemaj/REUTERS

blocks.text: "It is clear that the conditions do not exist for armed conflict, but there is a danger that the war could continue by other means," she said.
Future impact of the verdict
Asked how the verdict would affect relations between Serbia and Kosovo, lawyer Olenik recalled that previous judgments by international courts have had little impact in this regard.
"I hope things will be better now. That depends on the political elites in both countries," he said, adding that Kosovo society "has been pushed considerably to the right over the past four years."

"I am not optimistic that the verdict will have a positive effect in the near future," he said. "But I think that, as time passes — in 10 or 15 years — people will look at what has been established by these judgments in a more realistic manner and without such strong emotions."

blocks.text: Stat of the day: The world’s rivers experienced one of their driest years in more than three decades in 2025

blocks.caption: Only about a third of rivers were in the normal flow range in 2025, according to a study. Photograph: Darko Vojinović/AP

blocks.text: Last year was among the driest years on record for rivers across the world, with 36% of the global river basin area documenting river flows below or well below normal, according to an assessment of the global water cycle by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). Overall, the amount of freshwater held on or under the ground was 42% below normal across the world last year.
The Filter recommends: 14 easy upgrades to keep your home safe and secure

blocks.caption: The US Fire Administration recommends installing smoke alarms inside every bedroom, outside each separate sleeping area and on every level of the home. Photograph: Andriy Popov/Alamy

blocks.text: The Guardian’s Filter US team looks into the best home upgrades worth considering to keep your home safe and secure.
Don’t miss this: How the attention economy overwhelmed children’s TV

blocks.caption: Does your child’s favorite show give them a chance to reflect, or does it move too quickly for its lessons to sink in? Photograph: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Netflix/Fantorangen/Ludo Studio/Zach Hyman/ ZUMA Press, Inc./Apple TV

blocks.text: Pacing is everything when it comes to children’s entertainment, writes Natalia Kucirkova, a senior lecturer in early years and childhood studies at Manchester Metropolitan University – something that should be especially concerning in an attention economy that overwhelms and overshouts. When media moves too quickly, it risks losing the time needed for a child to make meaning. A child watching a character comfort a friend may not be able to recognize the repair or imagine doing the same thing with his or her own cohorts if the scene moves too quickly. A child must notice that another person feels something different in order for the child to develop empathy, Kucirkova writes – something that takes time.
… or this: 125,000 people displaced as war reignites in Yemen

blocks.caption: ‘We fled a large, comfortable home, and here we are struggling to find a plastic sheet and wooden poles,’ said Asma Taleb in al-Safia camp in Taiz, Yemen. Photograph: Nasser Al-Sakkaf/The Guardian

blocks.text: Renewed fighting in Yemen has displaced at least 125,000 people since the start of September 2026, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha). “This war doesn’t differentiate between people. Rich or poor, high class or low class, we all fled our homes on the same day,” said Asma Taleb, a woman in her 50s who left her home last week with her two sons and five grandchildren.
Climate check: Global heating was a destabilizing factor in the glacier collapse that caused the Nepal-Tibet floods

blocks.caption: ‘Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,’ said Dr Friederike Otto. Photograph: Suryams Upreti/AAP

blocks.text: Researchers found that the climate breakdown likely weakened the glacier that collapsed last month, causing catastrophic floods that killed hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet. In the region where the collapse happened, July and August 2026 were the warmest on record locally, reaching 5C above the 30-year average in the days before the collapse. In this region, the climate breakdown has caused about 2C of warming since preindustrial times.

Scientists believe this to be the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent, made over the course of eight months.

articles.title: Impeachment court issues show cause order on Ridon, Tolosa over sub judice rule
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court issued a show cause order on House prosecutor Terry Ridon and private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa, Jr., asking them to explain their statements that could violate the sub…

blocks.text: Published September 17, 2026 7:13pm

The Senate impeachment court issued a show cause order on House prosecutor Terry Ridon and private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa, Jr., asking them to explain their statements that could violate the sub judice rule, meaning the ban on parties from discussing the merits of the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte outside the trial proceedings.

This was confirmed by Ridon to reporters on Thursday, a day after the Senate impeachment court announced the issuance of the show cause orders on two members of the prosecution panel without naming names.

“We confirm that we received the show cause order from the Senate impeachment court concerning sub judice matters. We respect the decision of the Impeachment court, and we will answer the order by the end of today,” Ridon told reporters at the sidelines of the ongoing budget briefing.
“Aside from me, Atty. Tolosa was also given a show cause order, and he will also answer it by the end of the day,” Ridon added.

The sub judice rule is provided under Article 18 of the Rules on Impeachment, which states that the presiding officer, the members of the Senate, “shall refrain from making any comments and disclosures in public pertaining to the merits of a pending impeachment trial” and that “the same shall likewise apply to the prosecutors, the person impeached, and their respective counsel and witnesses.”

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero, back in August 2026, cautioned the parties against violating the sub judice rule by saying that violations going forward will have consequences, including a P30,000 fine per offense.
Ridon did not cite the specific statements that were flagged by the Senate impeachment court.
Instead, he stressed that it was the prosecutors’ duty to explain the impeachment process to the public within the rules set by the Impeachment court.

“Our role as prosecutors should be viewed in the entirety of the context of explaining to the public the goings-on of the trial. We have never asked the court to pre-judge. The impeachment trial is ongoing,” Ridon said.

“We do not seek to influence the senator-judges. Ultimately, ang pinakamahalaga po, hindi lang po kami-kami sa kapulungan. Ang pinakamahalaga po, nauunawaan ng ordinaryong Pilipino kung bakit kung meron po tayong paglilitis, bakit mahalaga po yung katotohanan, bakit mahalaga yung pananagutan,” Ridon added.

(The understanding of the process should not be limited to the members of Congress. The most important thing here is for the Filipino people to understand why there is a trial, why the truth matters, and why accountability is important.)
Ridon, however, said the prosecution will submit to the decision of the impeachment court.

“Whatever these statements [supposedly violating sub judice], we leave it to the court to make that determination. We don't want to debate with the court because they are the court,” Ridon added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: King Charles, Earl Spencer clash over Diana death once again
articles.summary: Buckingham Palace has rejected criticisms of King Charles III in a new book from the brother of his late wife Princess Diana. Earl Charles Spencer has been a fierce critic of his former…

image.caption: The feud between King Charles and Earl Charles Spencer, Princess Diana's brother, dates back to her death and funeral in 1997 — as do the latest allegations in Spencer's new bookImage: Gerry Penny/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Buckingham Palace has hit back at claims by the late Princess Diana's brother that King Charles III acted cruelly after her death in a car crash in 1997 — the latest of many criticisms leveled at the king by his former brother-in-law Earl Charles Spencer in recent decades.
The dispute is liable to overshadow a public engagement on Thursday when Charles will meet with various AI executives in Scotland to appeal to them to take care in their work.
What is the argument about?

Earl Spencer, Diana's elder brother, has written a new book being serialized in the Daily Mail newspaper, in which he alleges that Charles told him in an angry phone call, "rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough," days after Diana died aged 36.

"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," a palace spokesperson said late on Wednesday.
Charles and Diana had gone through an acrimonious separation prior to her death in 1997 and relations between the two Charles' were already at rock bottom prior to the late-night tragedy in Paris.

blocks.caption: Charles Spencer resides at the family estate Althrop House in NorthamptonshireImage: Jordan Pettitt/empics/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the book, "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," which is due to be published in full next week, Spencer repeats his assertion that he called for Princes William and Harry — then aged 15 and 12 — not to walk in the massive public funeral procession for their mother on September 6, 1997.
Spencer claims that Charles subjected him to a "stream of anger" after he raised this objection.

"He unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured', he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough!'," Spencer writes.

Diana's sudden death in a car crash as her chauffeur tried to evade paparazzi photographers led to an outpouring of grief in much of the UK and beyond for the popular if polarizing princess — known for her striking looks, a relatively easy manner by royal standards, and for her engagement with charitable causes. The monarchy faced accusations of failing to adequately respond in public to her death, particularly in the immediate aftermath.
The feud between the Spencers and the Windsors both before and particularly after her death has been a recurring feature in the British press and on popular TV shows like Netflix's "The Crown."

blocks.caption: Diana died a few months after this photo was taken, aged 36Image: John Stillwell/PA Wire/empics/picture alliance

blocks.text: Charles and Camilla in Scotland, set for AI event
Charles and Queen consort Camilla have been at Balmoral Castle in Scotland for most of September, attending a series of appointments amid their stay.

One of the higher profile engagements takes place on Thursday at Dumfries House in Ayrshire, where Charles is hosting executives from AI companies like Nvidia, Google DeepMind, Open AI and Anthropic, among others, at what's seen as a crucial time for the industry.

"The decisions taken at this ​formative time ‌will shape the world inherited by future generations," the King would say, according to excerpts released in advance by the palace. "The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world."
Britain's Minister for Artificial Intelligence Kanishka Narayan, promoted to a new bespoke ministerial role by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, will also attend the event.
So will Paolo Benanti, an adviser to Pope Leo XIV, who has demonstrated considerable interest, and indeed concern, in AI development.
