articles.title: Ed Sheeran reportedly donating $2M to 'aid in the region' amid Macklemore fallout
articles.summary: The billionaire stadium owner who allegedly led efforts to remove Macklemore as Ed Sheeran’s opening act over his pro-Palestinian comments onstage is now donating $2 million US in aid to "the region."

image.caption: U.K. singer Ed Sheeran, right, has reportedly donated $2 million US to aid the "humanitarian crisis" in the Middle East, according to the billionaire stadium owner who allegedly led efforts to remove Macklemore, left, as Sheeran's opening act over the U.S. rapper's pro-Palestinian comments onstage.

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

The billionaire stadium owner who allegedly led efforts to remove Macklemore as Ed Sheeran’s opening act over his pro-Palestinian comments onstage is now donating $2 million US in aid to "the region."
Macklemore pledges $1M to pro-Palestinian causes after tour ouster over comments

The billionaire stadium owner who allegedly led efforts to remove Macklemore as Ed Sheeran's opening act over his pro-Palestinian comments onstage is now donating $2 million US in aid to "the region."

The news came shortly after Macklemore announced plans Wednesday to donate $1 million US from his net earnings from the tour to six organizations helping Palestinians — including the UN agency for Palestinian refugees — and challenged Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft to do the same.

While Kraft did not specify in his statement where his funds would be going, and a spokesperson did not clarify, he said Sheeran had asked him to match a $2 million US donation from Sheeran "before Macklemore challenged me."

He also said that he wanted people to know that "for decades, I have supported efforts that create opportunity for Palestinians and have brought young Palestinians and Israelis together to build businesses, create jobs, and forge relationships."
Statement from Robert Kraft pic.twitter.com/as3f4RUKse—GilletteStadium

Benjamin Hammond Haggery, better known as Macklemore, opened for Sheeran for the first two U.S. shows on the Loop Tour on Sept. 4 and 5 at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. He was slated to open for the remaining eight of Sheeran's 10 U.S. shows, but announced in a lengthy Instagram post on Monday that he'd been dropped from the tour.

Macklemore's onstage remarks at MetLife — including chanting "Free Palestine" and expressing solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank — drew criticism from pro-Israel groups, including a petition calling for his removal.
Sheeran in hot water over consulting billionaire about Macklemore

Macklemore blamed his removal on Kraft, claiming Kraft said Macklemore would not be allowed onstage and rallied other stadium owners to threaten to cancel scheduled concerts if he was not taken off the bill.
Sheeran released his own statement on Tuesday, defending his choice not to take a public stance and saying he is "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine."
In the statement, Sheeran said, "Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine. Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me."
In response, Sheeran's remaining supporting acts all quit the tour.

items: Remaining supporting acts quit Ed Sheeran tour amid backlash over Macklemore ousting

blocks.text: The Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe were scheduled to replace Macklemore as the opening acts on Sheeran's remaining U.S. tour dates. Finneas, the American singer and close collaborator of his sister Billie Eilish, was scheduled to open for Sheeran on four of his South American dates. Beoga, an Irish folk band, had been performing with Sheeran for part of his set since the tour began in January in New Zealand.
"Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," Finneas wrote.

Graham also appeared to take a veiled shot at Kraft, writing: "Money doesn't give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody's bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we're allowed to acknowledge."

Sheeran hasn't posted since those supporting acts left the tour, and his representative didn't respond to an emailed request for comment. The promoter, Messina Touring Group, also hasn't responded to requests for comment.
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Trump calls EU offer to Canada of associate membership ‘laughable’, while threatening tariffs
articles.summary:
The US president call the move a ‘hostile act’, as Canada seeks to move closer to the EU and diversify its defence ties

Donald Trump has threatened the European Union with “serious tariffs”…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has threatened the European Union with “serious tariffs” and a cut to trade after the bloc proposed to make Canada its first ever associate member, calling the idea “laughable”.

Suggesting the move was a “hostile act”, the US president told reporters he could put “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member” on Wednesday, a day before Canadian prime minister Mark Carney was due to address the European parliament.

Von der Leyen pitched closer cooperation on tech, defence and energy to Carney, telling the European parliament that, as democracies face a “fracture in the international rules-based system”, Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together.

Canada and the EU already have a trade deal and numerous bilateral agreements, but have been moving closer since Donald Trump returned to the White House and raised tariffs on both old allies, while repeatedly talking about Canada becoming the 51st US state and lambasting the EU.

In a sign that Canada was seeking to further diversify its defence ties ⁠away from ⁠the ​United States, Carney’s office announced on Wednesday that the country had formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military ⁠coalition.
The force is ​a rapid response ‌military partnership comprised of 10 North Atlantic Nato member states, including Denmark, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden.

On Wednesday, Carney and British prime minister Andy Burnham held a bilateral meeting at the grounds of Everton football club. The leaders, who are both fans of the premiership club, then attended the team’s game against Wolves.

blocks.caption: Mark Carney and Andy Burnham pose for a picture ahead of an Everton match on Wednesday evening.  Photograph: Anthony Devlin/EPA

blocks.text: The two discussed deepening defence cooperation and the opportunities and ⁠challenges presented by ⁠artificial ​intelligence. Downing Street said both prime ministers emphasised the importance ​of building close ties with European partners, particularly on trade and defence.

The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, although it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, allowing deep economic integration with these countries, who follow many EU rules. However it remains to be seen what associate membership means, including for Canada’s relationship with the EU single market.
Von der Leyen said on Wednesday it was time to move from cooperation based on trade to a broader “alliance for the future” and “bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.
“We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project,” she said.

She listed energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, cyber and economic security as other fields of cooperation. “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: Labor backs down on veterans’ health services cap after furious backlash from Jacqui Lambie and ex-ADF members
articles.summary:
Independent senator had denounced as ‘cruel’ the plan to impose a $5,000 cap on allied health services for veterans

Labor has backdown on plans to impose a $5,000 cap on health services for…

blocks.text: Labor has backed down on plans to impose a $5,000 cap on health services for defence veterans, caving to growing political pressure after weeks of criticism.

The government announced it would no longer pursue the cap for allied health services, which had been to come into force on 1 July 2027, after a weeks-long campaign by the opposition, veterans’ groups and independent senator Jacqui Lambie.
In a surprise move on Thursday, the veterans’ affairs minister, Matt Keogh, said he would drop the plan after concerns were raised after the federal budget.
“We have been consulting on this measure and we have heard from veterans there are concerns about this approach,” Keogh said in a statement.
“We have been listening carefully and today the government is taking the proposed $5,000 threshold off the table.”
Keogh had been strongly criticised by veterans and the Coalition after he had initially refused to meet with a group of former servicemen lobbying for the changes to be scrapped.
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, has called on the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, to sack Keogh.

Labor had announced the policy to stop veterans being forced to go back to a doctor for an allied health referral every 12 sessions. The government said veterans needing more funding over the cap would still be allowed to apply for extra assistance.

Lambie had revealed her own health struggles and access to care in an impassioned speech to the Senate last month, urging the government to drop the $5,000 cap, warning it would have a “devastating impacts” on veterans.

blocks.caption: Jacqui Lambie shares prolapse story and slams veterans’ affairs women’s health services – video

blocks.text: “This cap was cruel, it was dangerous and it should never have been announced in the first place. I’m relieved that the government has finally listened and scrapped it and I thank them for doing it,” Lambie said on Thursday.
“This win belongs to every veteran, family member and Australian who spoke out, lobbied the government, signed the petition and kept the pressure on.
“They knew what would happen to our most vulnerable veterans if this cap went ahead and they fought like hell to make sure it didn’t.”
Taylor accused Keogh of not being up to the job and called the cap “egregious”.
“This was a mistake from the start. It should never have happened,” he said.
“These are people who are prepared to put themselves in harm’s way for our country, serving our country.
“This is a government that has had its priorities wrong from the moment we saw the budget. The budget is unwinding before our eyes.”
A Fair Care for Veterans spokesman, John Armfield, a former navy clearance diver, thanked Keogh for the backdown.
“This is what happens when a government listens to veterans,” he said.
“Veterans, families and doctors came from all over the country to say one thing: this cap would only ever hurt the most badly injured. Today the minister agreed, and we thank him for it.”
“Nobody had to lose for this to happen. The minister made the right call and he deserves credit for it.”

articles.title: Snapchat 'willing to implement' daily time limits for teens, boss tells BBC
articles.summary: Evan Speigel says it would be "an important step forward for the industry" in an interview with the BBC.

blocks.text: The boss of Snapchat says the firm would be "willing to implement" time limits for teens, following a call from Meta for it to take action.

Evan Spiegel told the BBC in an interview at the company's California headquarters that he believed setting a maximum amount of time that young users could spend on the app could be "an important step forward for the industry."
His comments came as the firm revealed a slew of new features for its upcoming Specs glasses, which it said could connect to Apple iPhone and Mac devices.
Meta has been pressuring other social media companies to join it in making platform changes it agreed to as part of a recent multi-billion dollar legal settlement with US states.
Instagram and Facebook-parent Meta was facing allegations from Attorneys General for most US states who said the firm deliberately designed its apps to be addictive to young users.

It agreed to pay $12.7bn and implement a two-hour daily limit for teen users across its platforms by default, in addition to muted notifications during school hours, blocks at night and other measures.

"I think it is an important step forward in the industry in terms of really identifying industry norms, and I think that would be beneficial overall," Spiegel told the BBC. "We've looked really thoughtfully at the terms."

As part of Meta's August settlement, the company said it would implement even more stringent time limits and pay an additional $5.3bn if YouTube and TikTok follow suit. It has denied any wrongdoing as part of the deal, which will be paid over a 10-year period.
Last month, a Meta spokesperson said it was hopeful that Snap would make similar platform changes as well.

Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap have all faced a barrage of litigation alleging their apps have helped spawn a youth mental health crisis. Snap has also been accused of facilitating illegal drug sales.
When asked about the idea of a default time limit, Spiegel said: "I think that's a really good example of something that that we'd be willing to implement."
But Spiegel did not commit to a timeline on when Snap might take action.
"That's something we've talked about internally," he said. "I don't have more to share today."
He noted that Snap offers tools through its Family Center feature, which currently enables parents to track aspects of how their teens are using Snapchat.
"We want to figure out how we can be part of the solution," Spiegel added.
YouTube-parent Google said it had no comment when asked if it planned to implement the measures in Meta's settlement. TikTok did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
Spiegel was talking to the BBC as Snapchat's parent Snap Inc announced new features for its upcoming Specs glasses.
He said the smart eyewear would use AI to suggest things for people to do based on what the tech learns about their goals, relationships and routines.

"Rather than the way that people use chatbots today where you constantly have to ask for stuff, Specs can understand what's important to you, and then offer recommendations or offer next steps," he said.
Like other smart glasses, Specs will use AI to let people see digital elements overlaid onto the world.
But the tech won't come cheap - retailing at $2,195 in the US and £1,995 in the UK.
"The target audience right now is early adopters of tech and developers as well as enterprise," Spiegel said.
With the device, Snap aims to offer a middle ground between VR headsets like Meta's Quest 3 and lightweight AI smart glasses offered by rivals which look more like conventional glasses.
"We're creating a totally new category here," said Spiegel.

"You have a really powerful computer that brings a lot of the immersive capability you see with VR, but they're also lightweight at just about 130 grams, so they're very wearable and they have these see-through lenses, so you can use them out in the world."
Specs is Snap's most recent foray into the wearable tech, coming a decade after its short-lived Spectacles cost the company tens of millions of dollars.
The device is also arriving as Meta is facing a significant backlash over its own smart glasses, which are estimated to be the most popular of the market.

Some online derisively call them "pervert glasses" over how they have been used to secretly film women, with one person telling the BBC they were filmed leaving the beach, while another said they were told to pay to remove a video of them from the internet.
Nevertheless, sales continue to rise. With seven million pairs having been sold according to Meta.
Snap said it has built into the design of Specs, which do not use facial recognition to identify people.
A white light flashes at the top of the glasses above the users nose when it is recording video and taking a photo.
The company says that will let people nearby see that recording is happening.
Users of Meta glasses have figured out ways to obscure components meant to indicate that a photo or video is being captured, including by tampering with the electronics in the device.
Meta says it has remotely disabled the cameras on thousands of its devices on which tampering or destruction of the indicator light was detected.

articles.title: How climate change worsened Nepal's deadly mountain collapse
articles.summary: A glacier and rock collapse in Nepal killed nearly 1,400 people and left thousands missing. Scientists say decades of warming helped set the disaster in motion.

image.caption: A drone view of flood damage along the Trishuli River in Nuwakot district, Nepal.Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nearly 1,400 people have died after a mountain slope collapsed and flash floods swept through the valleys of Nepal and Tibet. More than 5,000 people remain missing.

The collapse was initially thought to have been caused by an earthquake. Now, glaciologists and climate scientists have determined that a complex series of factors led to the disaster, with climate change laying the groundwork several times over: Warming temperatures receded the glacier, thawed permafrost and increased meltwater, destabilizing the slope until it gave way on August 26.

"This was not a single trigger event," Walter Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, told journalists on a press call. "The failure occurred at an elevation of about 5150 meters (about 16,896 feet) and there were several processes acting together over time scales of years to decades, rather than one factor acting alone."

blocks.caption: With no time to prepare, families in Devighat returned to mud-filled homes days later to salvage whatever survivedImage: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: How the disaster unfolded

The floods began upstream with a large rock avalanche on the north face of Langtang Lirung. That caused a section of the glacier to collapse at the same time, sending roughly 110 million cubic meters of rock and glacier ice, the size of 44,000 Olympic swimming pools, hurtling downward. That type of rock avalanche is rare, occurring at this size only once every 1,000-10,000 years.

The material fell about 1,400 meters (4,593 feet) from the mountain to the valley floor, picking up debris, water, ice, rock and sediment as it descended. The impact released as much energy as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. As it crashed into the valley, it also tore up buried glacier ice, adding up to 30 million more cubic meters of debris and water to the flow.

Within about seven minutes, the flood reached Nepal and China's Rasuwagadhi border, 20 kilometers (about 12 miles) downstream, moving at an average speed of 170 kilometers per hour (about 106 miles per hour). The flood continued downstream, traveling 200 kilometers in under seven hours.

blocks.caption: Relatives are going through photographs of missing people, trying to find loved onesImage: Safal Prakash Shrestha/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: How did this happen?

It was a complex combination of conditions, exacerbated by climate change, that allowed the slope to collapse in the first place. That's according to researchers with World Weather Attribution, an international collaboration of scientists that looks at the role of climate change in extreme weather and disaster events.
Rising temperatures, due to the burning of fossil fuels, have reshaped this stretch of the Himalayas for decades.

Near the failure site, the glacier's edge had retreated just 75 meters between 1964 and 2000. But between 2010 and 2026, it dramatically accelerated, retreating another 373 meters. That stripped away the ice supporting the rock wall above it.

Permafrost — or permanently frozen ground within the rock — had also started to thaw. That took place between 4,500 and 5,500 meters of elevation, a critical band that's most sensitive to warming. As it thawed, the mountain walls became more and more unstable.

In the immediate run-up to the collapse, conditions were extreme. July and August overall were the warmest on record in the area, with climate change adding about 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to the region. On August 24 and 25, temperatures ran roughly 2.5 to 2.7 degrees Celsius above the 10-year average. A day before the catastrophe unfolded, the maximum temperature was approximately 7 degrees Celsius above the reference mean.
An unusually snowy October in 2025 likely also played a role, generating more meltwater.

Researchers also believe a 2015 earthquake played a role. That magnitude-7.8 quake triggered an earlier avalanche at Langtang Lirung, which may have weakened the rock mass in the years since, priming the slope for failure.
A disaster beyond adaptation

Researchers also tried to find out whether this was a disaster the region could have prepared for and adapted to. They determined it was uniquely hard to detect, as Nepal's early warning systems are designed for forecastable rainfall-driven floods, not quickly developing, cascading events like this one.
Essentially, this kind of complex threat exceeds the limits of adaptation.

The flood outran Nepal's early warning systems and destroyed several monitoring gauges in its wake. The first mass SMS warning was sent about 38 minutes after the initial collapse, but the flood had already reached the border 7 minutes in.

"When warming destabilizes the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction," Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said.
"Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come."
After Nepal floods, survivors return to ruins of their homes

articles.title: Climate crisis likely behind devastating Nepal-Tibet floods that killed more than 1,300, first study finds
articles.summary:
Scientists say global heating was a destabilising factor in collapse of 200,000 sq metre glacier in August

Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic…

blocks.text: Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found.

Researchers identified unusually warm conditions before the glacier’s collapse, which sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres (3,885 cu ft) of snow and ice into the valley below. This triggered flash floods on an almost unprecedented scale, hitting communities downstream without warning.

“Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,” said Dr Friederike Otto, a climate science professor at Imperial College London, which carried out the study.

“When warming destabilises the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction. Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come.”

blocks.caption: A impromptu memorial in Kathmandu commemorates some of the people killed in the flooding. Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA

blocks.text: More than 1,300 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing after a massive section of overhanging glacier and rock measuring roughly 200,000 sq metres (2,153,000 sq ft) fell from Langtang Lirung mountain on 26 August.

It dropped about 1,400 metres (4,660ft), slamming into the valley floor with such intensity that it registered as an earthquake, liquidising ice and sparking a freezing flood that careened downriver at speeds exceeding 110 mph.
The devastating flood of water, ice, rock and sediment swept away families, homes, settlements, roads, bridges and other infrastructure, leaving survivors stranded and cut off.

“Rock avalanches of this size are rare, with annual frequency estimates of approximately one event this size every 1,000–10,000 years,” the study said. “This event shows that limits to adaptation are already being reached.”

The research was unlike previous studies by Otto and her team at World Weather Attribution (WWA) – a collaborative project between Imperial and other climate specialists worldwide – in that the role of climate breakdown could not be ascribed to one particular weather event.
Instead, the researchers found the disaster was the result of a compound crisis, with a number of factors made worse by decades of atmospheric heating as a result of greenhouse gas pollution.

Dr Ben Clarke, who researches extreme weather and climate change at Imperial, said the “fingerprints of climate change” were clear in the long-term changes that happened around the glacier before its catastrophic collapse.

blocks.caption: ‘Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,’ said Dr Friederike Otto. Photograph: Suryams Upreti/AAP

blocks.text: Among the study’s key findings were:
after newsletter promotion

items: In the region where the collapse happened, climate breakdown has caused about 2C of warming since pre-industrial times, and about 1.5C of warming in July and August specifically;
July and August 2026 were the warmest on record locally, reaching 5C above the 30-year average in the days before the collapse;
The freezing threshold in the Himalayas has risen by about 100 metres per decade since the 1980s, with higher and longer thaw temperatures weakening mountain slopes shaped by permafrost;
The warming temperature had already driven substantial glacier recession, removing stabilising ice from around the site where the collapse occurred and contributing meltwater;
A 7.8 magnitude earthquake in 2015 further contributed to slope failure, though its specific contribution to the disaster in August could not be confirmed.

blocks.text: Otto, Clarke and the WWA team said their study did not directly ascribe climate breakdown as the fundamental cause of the catastrophe. Instead, it was best understood as a destabilising factor on the existing geology.
Clarke said: “We found that climate change is transforming the high mountain environment, influencing many of the possible drivers of this collapse.”

blocks.caption: A major earthquake in Nepal in 2015 may also have contributed to the glacier’s collapse. Photograph: Ishwar Rauniyar/The Guardian

blocks.text: Nepal has filed a formal request with the UN loss and damage fund for financial support to address the destruction caused by the flood, a process that requires proof of a link to the climate crisis. The country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, has also demanded that top emitting nations such as China and India “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for the disaster.

Madhab Uprety, senior technical advisor for the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, which is part of WWA, said only aggressive cuts to global emissions could begin to address the “losses and damages faced by vulnerable frontline communities”.

He added: “In addition to the human tragedy on an unimaginable scale, the cost of recovery for this disaster is substantial. For a nation that’s done virtually nothing to contribute to this problem, it underlines the need to find fairness in helping climate vulnerable nations cope with the problems they have not unleashed.”

articles.title: Canada wants into Britain's rapid-response defence club
articles.summary: Canada has formally applied to join the United Kingdom's Joint Expeditionary Force, reversing a decision made more than a decade ago. Born from the Afghanistan war and reshaped by Russia's invasion…

image.caption: Canadian Armed Forces members are seen participating in drills in Cambridge Bay, Nunavut, in February. (Carlos Osorio/Reuters)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Canada has formally applied to join the United Kingdom's Joint Expeditionary Force, reversing a decision made more than a decade ago. Born from the Afghanistan war and reshaped by Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the coalition promises speed and flexibility — but raises an old question about what Canada is actually committing itself to.
Formal application to Joint Expeditionary Force announced during Carney's U.K. visit
Canada has formally applied to join the U.K.-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), a collection of NATO nations whose mandate is to respond more quickly in a crisis.
Prime Minister Mark Carney formally announced the plan on Wednesday while meeting with his British counterpart Andy Burnham.

In a statement, Carney called JEF an "important initiative" and highlighted other close defence ties with the U.K., including Canada's observer status in the development of the next generation of fighter jet.

Canada was asked by the U.K. more than dozen years ago to join JEF after it was formed in the waning days of the war in Afghanistan. The concept was discussed at the 2014 NATO leaders' summit in Wales, but ultimately the government of former prime minister Stephen Harper rebuffed the overtures.

items: Canada joining international program to build next generation of fighter jets
Canada urges U.K. to join new global bank for defence projects

blocks.text: The Canadian military, at the time in the throes of deep budget cuts by Conservative government of the day, was also deeply reluctant to join.

In an interview with The Canadian Press at the time, the commander of the military's joint operations command, Lt.-Gen. Jonathan Vance, who later became the chief of the defence staff, said there were a number of concerns about joining the British expeditionary force.

It would be, he said, a substantial undertaking for the military and could bind the country to respond in a specific way to a future crisis when the federal government might favour a different course.
Joining the force without a specific mission, Vance said in 2014, would signal "a commitment to future operations, having done the training, that you may — or may not — be able to honour."

In his statement on Wednesday, Carney did not say how Canada's participation in JEF would work on a practical level. And the country's current top military commander, Gen. Jennie Carignan, has yet to weigh in on what the membership might mean.
As it was originally conceived, the Joint Expeditionary Force was meant to preserve battlefield relationships that grew up during the Afghan war.

In 2012, Britain's then chief of defence staff, Gen. Sir David Richards, described a future force that could deploy rapidly overseas without Britain having to assemble an entirely new coalition for every crisis.
It was thought at the time that the British Army would provide the command structure and much of the military backbone and other countries would bring forces that plug into JEF as needed.
Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 gave the idea urgency.

At the NATO summit in Wales that year, Britain, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands and Norway formally agreed to establish JEF under NATO's new Framework Nations Concept. Finland and Sweden joined in 2017, before either country belonged to NATO, and Iceland entered the fold in 2021.
There is an important distinction to make. While JEF is made up of NATO nations, the organization has no equivalent of NATO's Article 5 collective defence clause.

items: First phase of Army restructuring creates division focused on defending Canada
Canada, Ukraine forge 100-year pact built on drones and defence
No longer taboo, Canada's defence industry steps into Europe's spotlight

blocks.text: It is essentially a coalition of willing states that can assemble forces for a particular contingency without requiring consensus among all NATO members.
There have been a series of military exercises held under the JEF banner since 2018.
But Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 turned JEF from an expeditionary military concept into something approaching a Northern European security coalition.

A 2024 research report by the U.K.-based Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) argued that JEF had genuine advantages, notably speed of decision-making compared with NATO, but it has not been seriously tested politically or operationally.
The study said that the expeditionary force is not actually a standing military body and governments provide forces when required.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

articles.title: Gordie Howe bridge vehicle traffic tops 340,000 in first full month of operation
articles.summary: Traffic at the new Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Windsor, Ont., and Detroit topped 340,000 in its first full month of operation, according to new data.

image.caption: The Gordie Howe International Bridge connects Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, adding a publicly-owned competition to the privately-owned Ambassador Bridge. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: Windsor·New
Traffic at the new Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Windsor, Ont., and Detroit topped 340,000 in its first full month of operation, according to new data.
New bridge traffic was nearly on par with nearby Ambassador Bridge
There were 343,507 crossings at the bridge in August, the first full month it was open, per fresh figures from the Bridge and Tunnel Operators Association.
It was nearly the same as traffic at the nearby Ambassador Bridge, which saw 345,445 crossings last month.
But the composition of the traffic on the competing spans was different. The majority of crossings at the Gordie Howe bridge were passenger vehicles: Nearly 270,000 vs. roughly 74,000 trucks.
At the Ambassador, truck traffic was around 150,000, compared to 196,000 passenger cars.

items: Ambassador Bridge 'aggressively' pursued trucking clients amid Gordie Howe delay: industry rep
New bridge, same traffic: Why is the road to the Ambassador Bridge still packed with trucks?

blocks.text: Jason Miller, a supply chain management professor at Michigan State University, says he believes many trucking companies have toll price contracts with the Ambassador Bridge.

"So what's happening is they are probably locked in for this year," he told Windsor Morning on Wednesday. "So it does not make as much sense for them to shift trucks over to Gordie Howe until they would have some type of renegotiated contract or they themselves have a contractual price with Gordie Howe."
LISTEN | Gordie Howe bridge attracts more cars than trucks in first full month of operation:
Windsor Morning6:52Gordie Howe Bridge attracts more cars than trucks in first full month of operation
The Windsor-Detroit Tunnel still had the highest volume of passenger vehicles, with approximately 280,000 crossings in August.
StatsCan data offers different look
Recently released numbers from Statistics Canada offer a more detailed look at the origin of the people crossing the various ports of entry in the Windsor-Detroit corridor.

"In August, the Gordie Howe International Bridge was used for 134,900 Canadian-resident return trips from the United States by automobile, 56.7 per cent of which were same-day," the federal agency said Friday. "It was also used as a port of entry for 101,000 US-resident trips to Canada by automobile, 52.2 per cent of which were same-day.
"During the same period, 348,000 Canadian and US residents entered Canada by automobile at Windsor's Ambassador Bridge and the Windsor-Detroit Tunnel, down 35.4 per cent from August 2025."
The agency also said that 34,800 commercial transport trucks entered Canada using the Gordie Howe Bridge last month.
"Commercial transport truck entries at Windsor's other ports increased by 0.4 per cent from the same period one year earlier to total 87,400," it added.
Miller said traffic volumes at the three crossings are likely to shift in the months ahead as the "novelty effect" of taking the brand new Gordie Howe bridge wears off.
In any case, he said the traffic volumes at the new span being nearly as high as those at the Ambassador Bridge show "the need for that second crossing."

blocks.text: "What I'm really curious to see is if there's any information [to] come out about the wait times at either bridge, because that that to me is the most important thing beyond just the crossings, is just that smoother flow of commerce," he added.

articles.title: US interest rates raised for first time in three years
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve unanimously voted to increase interest rates to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75% on Wednesday.

blocks.text: US interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years and could be increased further in a bid to slow rising prices.
Rates were hiked to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75% by the Federal Reserve in a unanimous decision on Wednesday despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the move was because "inflation is too high and has been for too long", adding that it was a "sober" and "responsible decision".
However, Trump said rates "should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World - BY FAR".
Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for people wanting to secure loans, mortgages and credit cards, but can lead to better returns on savings.
Warsh said while there was "an attitude of optimism" within the Federal Reserve leadership, inflation remained a problem.
"For more than five years, inflation has been running above target," he said. "The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long."
Central banks tend to increase rates when inflation is high to discourage spending and encourage saving in the hope this will reduce the pace of price rises.
But it's a balancing act, as higher rates can also encourage businesses to hold off on investing and hurt economic growth.

Ahead of the mid-term elections in November, affordability is one of the top concerns of American voters, who have seen diesel prices hit an all-time high and petrol rise above $4 (£2.99) a gallon on average.
Global oil prices have surged since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran, driving up the price of car fuel as well as the cost of goods and services generally.

Warsh told a press conference following the decision to raise interest rates that the Fed "cannot affect any individual price whether it be oil prices, whether it be food stuffs at the grocery store", but could ensure price rises do not broaden across the economy.
He added that strong jobs market and wider economy meant the Fed was focused on stablising prices, adding that those least well off had most to gain from lower inflation.

Asked about the message the decision sent to Trump, Warsh chuckled before saying "I have got nothing for you on a discussion with the president," as he batted away similar questions with the same response.
The Federal Reserve is independent of the government, but has faced sharp criticism from Trump over its decisions on rates in recent years.
Trump was heavily critical of Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell, who stepped down at the end of his term earlier this year, for not cutting rates.
Following Wednesday's announcement, Trump said rates should be cut to "1%, or less".
"LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!", he posted on social media.

Earlier a White House press secretary Kush Desai told Fox News the president and White House had "reiterated our commitment to the independence of the Federal Reserve on numerous occasions" but added it did not prevent Trump being able to voice his opinions.
Warsh said at the press conference that "part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane".
This hike by the Fed is the first move rate move in any direction since they were cut in December 2025. The last time they were raised was in July 2023.
A 0.25pp increase will likely add to increasing mortgage rates for homebuyers, as the rates set by banks and other lenders are heavily influenced by the Fed's policy rate.
Major US banks JP Morgan, KeyCorp and BNY raised their prime lending rate on Wednesday to 7% from 6.75% in response, which will rates charged on credit cards and personal loans.
Mortgage costs have climbed over the past year but remain below peaks seen in 2023. A 30-year fixed deal is 6.76% on average, while a 15-year deal is 6.09%, according to figures from Freddie Mac.

Due to many US homeowners having 30-year and 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, changes to interest rates will not impact monthly repayments, though they could affect those looking to secure a loan for a home or refinance.

Warsh declined to provide his own view on where he saw interest rates going into the future, but the majority of his fellow policymakers said they believe rates would be hiked again before the end of this year to between 4-4.25%.
A small majority said rates could rise further to the 4.25-4.5% next year, before cuts begin in 2028 and 2029.
The forecast suggested price rises will ease in the coming years, with inflation, the measure used to assess the cost of living, predicted to fall steadily to the Fed's 2% target by 2029.

The US is not alone in tackling the inflation impact from the conflict in the Middle East, with the European Central Bank raising rates last week and the Bank of England set to make its own decision on Thursday.

blocks.text: Albanese government to improve safety in child support system

blocks.caption: Tom McIlroy

blocks.text: Tom McIlroy
Tanya Plibersek and Katy Gallagher have announced plans to close gaps that have allowed family and domestic violence perpetrators to continue causing harm through the child support system.

The new rules will scrap legal requirements that any information provided by one parent be shared with the other parent, stopping situations where sharing that information could put children or a parent at risk.

Families will also be supported to recover more unpaid child support debts when they move into official arrangements, and new rules will be created to remove the harm that can arise from family tax benefit debts caused by child support payers against their former partners.
In a joint statement, the social services minister and the finance minister said:

double quotation markThere is almost $2 billion of unpaid child support in this country. There are almost 100,000 parents and carers in the child support system who have experienced or are at risk of experiencing family and domestic violence. Australian children deserve better. This is the first stage of the most significant reforms to child support in decades, helping create a system that is safer, simpler and more effective for Australian families.
Australia breaks into top 10 global gender gap rankings

blocks.caption: Ima Caldwell

blocks.text: Ima Caldwell
Australia has broken into the top 10 of the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Report, ranking eighth out of 148 countries – its highest ranking ever.
The 2026 report marks a significant climb for Australia, moving up 35 places from 43rd since the Albanese government took office.

The government credits this historic high to improved political representation (including a majority-female cabinet), expanded paid parental leave, wage increases in female-dominated sectors and new investments in women’s health.
Anthony Albanese said in a statement that the ranking “slipped to an all-time low of 50th under the previous Coalition government” and acknowledged that the work must continue:

double quotation markThe job is not done and we will continue to focus our efforts on lifting wages, ending gender-based violence, increasing female representation in workplaces, investing in women’s health and more.
The minister for women, Katy Gallagher, said the record ranking was “not by accident”, also recognising areas for improvement:

double quotation markWe know there is more work to do across our priorities of ending violence against women, valuing care, improving women’s economic empowerment, improving women’s health outcomes and strengthening women’s leadership and representation – this is just one measure that shows Australia is moving in the right direction.

blocks.caption: Katy Gallagher. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP

blocks.text: International student visa changes expected
International students will see some of the biggest changes in the reform of immigration settings.

Last year Australia issued more than 337,000 international student visas, of which about 45,000 went to dependents or family members of the primary applicant. The vast majority of students will now be expected to be required to come alone.
Burke gave a preview in parliament yesterday.

double quotation markWe do need to get net overseas migration down. We need to make sure that we deal with the numbers overall, and do so in a sensible, a targeted way that provides the easiest pathway through the Australian economy.
Burke’s speech kicks off at 12.30pm today.
Long-anticipated immigration changes drop today
Foreign students will face tough restrictions on the ability to bring family members into Australia under big changes to the country’s immigration system.
The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, will reveal the changes today at the National Press Club, after plans for a speech more than a month ago were derailed.
Burke’s plan is designed to bring down net overseas migration (Nom) while doing the least damage to the economy.
His speech is titled: “The work of managing the migration program: Who arrives, who stays, who leaves”.

The plan will shift some rules for visa categories away from demand-driven settings, introduced during the Howard government, allowing more control on the numbers of people coming into, and departing, the country.
Labor plans to use legislation to gain more control over arrival numbers but could rely on regulation and directives to departmental officials if it cannot find agreement in parliament.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.

Foreign students will face tough restrictions on the ability to bring family members into Australia under big changes to the country’s immigration system to be announced at the National Press Club this lunchtime by Tony Burke. More details coming up.

articles.title: Key House Democrat refuses to clear Trump’s $2.8bn arms sale to Israel
articles.summary:
Pro-Israel Gregory Meeks raises concerns over threat to civilian lives from package of 40,000 one-ton bombs

The top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee has thrown up a roadblock…

blocks.text: The top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee has thrown up a roadblock to one of the largest US arms transfers of Trump’s second term, refusing to clear a $2.8bn sale of 2,000lb bombs to Israel.
Gregory Meeks announced the hold on Tuesday on a package of 40,000 of the bombs, among the most destructive conventional munitions in the US arsenal.

“The Trump administration has not provided sufficient assurances that these weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with US law and with appropriate protections for civilians,” he said. “I therefore will not clear this sale at this time.”
The deal, funded through US Foreign Military Financing, covers 20,000 MK-84 bombs, 20,000 BLU-117 bombs and 20,000 I-2000 penetrator warheads.

Meeks cannot single-handedly veto the $2.8bn arms transfer, but his leverage comes from the informal custom of “tiered review”. Under this practice, the state department submits major weapons packages to top foreign affairs lawmakers for an informal sign-off before triggering a formal notification to Congress. Killing the sale outright would need a veto-proof joint resolution of disapproval in both chambers, a bar Congress has not cleared. A similar push by Senator Bernie Sanders failed along party lines in April.

In 2025, the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, declared a national security emergency to bypass congressional review and fast-track nearly $3bn in weapons, including more than 35,000 heavy bombs and 4,000 bunker-buster warheads. With a separate $6.67bn package in January, the administration has now cleared or expedited over $12bn in arms for Israel since Trump took office. Meeks has said the pace has outrun oversight, accusing officials of skipping briefings and rushing sales while raising alarms over Israeli conduct in the occupied West Bank and Lebanon.

The hold also lands amid longstanding accusations that Israel has used American weapons unlawfully. The Leahy laws bar US assistance to foreign military units credibly linked to extrajudicial killings and serious abuse; the state department in 2024 flagged at least five Israeli units on those grounds before the war in Gaza even began, including one battalion tied to the death of a Palestinian American at a West Bank checkpoint.

The Geneva conventions, meanwhile, bar arming a party where there is a clear risk of war crimes – a standard a UN commission of inquiry cited last year in finding Israel’s Gaza campaign amounted to genocide and calling on the US and other states to halt weapons transfers. In 2024, Biden administration lawyers, including some at the state department, had concluded it was reasonable to assess that Israel had violated international humanitarian law and Leahy laws by using American weapons in Gaza, even as the administration publicly avoided making that determination.
Meeks, long known for his strong pro-Israel views, emphasized that the hold was not a break with the country itself.

“This decision does not diminish congressional support for Israel’s legitimate defense needs,” he said. “It reflects Congress’s responsibility to ensure that US-funded weapons are used lawfully, responsibly and with meaningful safeguards for human life.”
The state department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Maritime experts urge use of verified weather reports after kayaker capsizes in B.C. waters
articles.summary: Jonathan Levine considers himself lucky to be alive after his kayak capsized in the ocean during what he thought would be a leisurely paddle in Howe Sound.

image.caption: The Levines went for a morning paddle on Sunday, Sept. 13, and ended up caught in large waves off Minaty Bay near Britannia Beach. (Jane Levine)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Jonathan Levine considers himself lucky to be alive after his kayak capsized in the ocean during what he thought would be a leisurely paddle in Howe Sound.
Strangers rescue B.C. man from ocean after kayak flips in tall waves
Maritime first responders are advising against using AI chatbots for weather reports following a close call for a paddler on B.C.'s South Coast.
Levine and his wife Jane were eager to go for a morning kayak paddle on Sunday, as they’ve done many times, from their home in Furry Creek, about 35 kilometres north of Vancouver.
They tried to use an AI chatbot to determine the safest time to paddle after finding it difficult to get concise information online.
“We proceeded in the direction of Britannia Beach, as ChatGPT had suggested to my wife,” Levine said.
At first, it was sunny and seemingly calm, so the couple decided to stay out longer than planned.
That’s when they got into trouble.
“I hit these massive waves that came from nowhere. They were at least about five, six feet in height, and my kayak was rocking and rolling all over the place,” Levine said.

items: More stories from Vancouver-South Coast

blocks.text: The Howe Sound commonly experiences strong winds in the afternoon on warm days due to the coastal fjords along and temperature differences. There can also be fairly strong currents due to the strong river outflow.
B.C. man pulled from ocean by boaters after kayak capsizes
As the couple rounded the corner at Minaty Bay, Levine's kayak flipped, sending him plunging into the waves.
“The life-jacket was almost like trying to be wrenched off my body, basically because of the actual wave movement,” Levine said.
He tried over and over again to swim to the shore.
“Every time I kept swimming in one direction, [the waves] kept pushing me back,” Levine said.
Levine tried to stay calm while getting battered by waves for 15 minutes.
“I think as a human being aged 71, part of the advantages of being an old man is that you are probably quite clever in dangerous situations,” Levine said.
His wife, who was in another kayak, shouted to nearby boats and used her cellphone to call for help.
Strangers spot capsized kayak
Long-time sailor Adrian Ward and his friend, local firefighter Travis Welsh, were out for a boat ride near Minaty Bay when Ward noticed the bottom of the kayak floating amid the waves.
“As we approach, we're starting to see waves crashing over his head,” Ward said.
The conditions caught Ward and Welsh off guard.
“We were just getting lifted up and down, six feet at a time, and it came on really quickly,” Ward said.
Ward and his friend pulled Levine out of the water and onto their boat.
“He was really tired and a bit cold, not too cold, luckily,” Ward said. “Just really happy that it had a good outcome for the guy and that he got to go home.”
Levine was not injured and said the two strangers managed to get his kayak out safely, too.
“The two men were incredible, they calmed me down, they knew exactly what to do, they were so helpful,” Levine said.
His wife paddled safely to shore.
“She was a superwoman,” Levine said. “Without Jane, I wouldn't be alive.”
Staying safe on the water
Experts suggest checking multiple reports from verified sources for wind, tides and currents, rather than relying on artificial intelligence.

“Checking Environment Canada is important because they still have actual human eyes on those forecasts that understand thermal inflows and outflows,” said Scott Shaw-MacLaren, the coxswain with Squamish’s Royal Canadian Marine Search and Rescue.
“If you do, like, anything with AI, verify sources and read it for yourself.”
Shaw-MacLaren also suggests always having a marine VHF radio, as it’s the fastest way to alert other boaters if in trouble.

items: 2 boaters rescued after fishing vessel sinks between B.C.'s Lower Mainland and Vancouver Island

blocks.text: Brehnen Rowell, Officer in Charge at the Victoria Lifeboat Station with the Canadian Coast Guard, also recommends using multiple different sources and, in particular, the Government of Canada website.
“That’s really key for making sure you're staying safe out there, is making sure that you're aware of the currents and tides,” Rowell said.
Rowell said making a plan before heading out on the water and sticking to it is also important
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Alanna Kelly is a CBC News journalist based in Squamish, B.C., covering the Sea-to-Sky region, including Whistler, Pemberton and the Sunshine Coast. You can email story ideas to alanna.kelly@cbc.ca.

articles.title: US House votes to hold billionaire Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt
articles.summary: Black - who had business ties to Epstein - declined to appear and provide documents related to the convicted sex offender.

blocks.text: The US House of Representatives has agreed to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for defying legal summons related to its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Black - who had business ties to Epstein - did not comply with a subpoena ordering him to appear before the House Oversight Committee earlier this month and share documents related to Epstein.
Lawyers for Black, who has sued over the summons, called the contempt move "outrageous".
After passage of the measure holding Black in contempt, Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer said: "No one is above the law."
"We will continue to seek transparency for the American people and justice for survivors."
In a statement shared with US media, lawyers for Black called the House move an "outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr. Black".

"The full House is holding him in contempt without any regard to the active litigation challenging the lawfulness of the Committee's actions and the ethics complaint against Chairman Comer," they said.
The measure, which passed by unanimous consent, means the matter will be referred to the US justice department, which will decide whether to criminally prosecute Black.
In a statement, the committee's top Democrat, Congressman Robert Garcia, called the contempt vote "an important step towards justice and accountability".
"We will continue to center the survivors in our fight to hold those responsible for these horrific crimes," he said.
Black walked out of voluntary testimony before the House Oversight Committee in June after he was asked about nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) he may have signed, lawmakers said at the time.
Black left Apollo Global Management, which he co-founded, amid scrutiny in 2021 over his Epstein ties. He has denied any wrongdoing with regards to his dealings with Epstein.
The subpoenas, which ordered Black to share NDAs and give an on-camera deposition under oath, were issued after he left the committee meeting in June.
Black has said he hired Epstein as a wealth management adviser, telling lawmakers in June that he gave Epstein $158m (£118m) for legitimate reasons.
The billionaire has said he did not know about Epstein's crimes until he was charged with sex trafficking in July 2019.

articles.title: ‘Made in Europe’ laws could derail UK plans for reset with EU
articles.summary:
Government sources say legislation aimed at China poses a risk to British businesses and must be addressed

European legislation that threatens to lock British business out of EU industry…

blocks.text: European legislation that threatens to lock British business out of EU industry could derail a planned reset summit between the bloc and the UK, government sources have said.

The “Made in Europe” legislation – formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act – is designed to curb China’s increasing presence in European industry, but was not on the reset plan agreed by the former prime minister, Keir Starmer, and the European Commission chief, Ursula von der Leyen, in London in May 2025.

A follow-up summit was due to be held in July this year, but was cancelled after Starmer’s resignation. The government is now looking to change the agenda, with one source saying that “Made in Europe should be on the agenda”.

It is understood that Hamish Falconer, the new cabinet minister with responsibility for the reset, told the EU’s trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, this was the UK’s new priority when the pair met last week.

On Tuesday, the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, told a gathering of UK business leaders on Tuesday they needed to let their EU partners know the risks posed by Made in Europe, which will prioritise EU suppliers in key industries including car manufacturing and defence.

Ministers have privately expressed fears that the reset has lost significant momentum since Andy Burnham became prime minister, with his focus on the domestic agenda. Agreements have yet to be reached on several key issues, including what tuition fees will be paid by EU students coming to the UK on a mooted “youth experience” programme.

blocks.caption: Keir Starmer and Ursula von der Leyen set out plans for a UK-EU reset in London in May 2025. Photograph: Carl Court/PA

blocks.text: UK sources say that while a food and drink deal and a youth mobility scheme are still on the agenda, the government will not agree to a new summit date until the bigger issues of the Industrial Accelerator Act are included in discussions.
There was talk in London and Brussels that a meeting could be convened on 6 November, but it is understood this could now be pushed backuntil the end of November or beyond.

One government source said: “We are willing to negotiate on the things that matter to them, but they have to be able to negotiate the thing that matters to us. Made in Europe should be on the table, definitely.”
The UK fears the Made in Europe laws could jeopardise billions of pounds worth of trade if British goods are not categorised as European, locking it out of key contracts on the continent.
France, which conceived the Made in Europe laws, is pushing to have the legislation passed by the end of the year, deepening fears that British manufacturing could be left behind.

It is thought that France is sympathetic to the UK’s position, but believes increasing competition from China makes it more important to get the legislation on the books now, and make allowances for third countries later, a process that could take years.

blocks.caption: A Chinese-made electric bus on the streets of Copenhagen, Denmark. Photograph: Francis Joseph Dean/Dean Pictures/Alamy

blocks.text: One EU diplomat said that there was substantial backing among key member states for the UK to be included in Made in Europe, though not all agreed.
“The problem is the benefits are seen as asymmetrical,” the diplomat said. “The UK gets more out of it than the EU.”
It is understood the Netherlands, Germany, Poland and Italy are all in favour of the UK’s inclusion, but France remains unconvinced.
The government’s newly assertive approach could give the UK some leverage in negotiations over concessions on youth mobility, something that is a political priority for many EU capitals.
Another UK source said a deal on Made in Europe would be “a good faith demonstration that we can find answers and almost everything else”.
A government spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and trusted European partner, committed to our shared security and economic cooperation.
“We will continue to engage with the EU on Made in Europe and work together, as like-minded partners, to boost growth and open up trade.”
The UK’s desire for a deal on manufacturing rules comes at time when the EU is under pressure from industry across the bloc to loosen China’s growing presence in supply chains.
after newsletter promotion
Last week, manufacturing bosses warned of a potential loss of 300,000 jobs this year unless incentives are put in place to make European products more attractive than cheaper parts from China.
The EU’s deficit with China is now running at €1bn a day, with fears that European companies are being cannibalised from within.
In her state of the union address to the European parliament on Wednesday, Von der Leyen said the EU needed to grow non-Chinese supplies of rare earths and critical minerals vital to manufacturing.
Her surprise offer of an associate membership deal with Canada demonstrated how far Brussels can go to court third country partners.

Speaking in the presence of the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, the EU chief said: “We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. We must urgently reimagine our partnerships.”

The EU and Canada are due to hold a summit in late October to develop their future relationship. The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, though it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, enabling deep economic integration with these countries, which follow many EU rules including free movement – a red line for the UK.
Carney, who is due to address the European parliament on Thursday, has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU, as his country seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade.

blocks.caption: Mark Carney and Andy Burnham in Liverpool on Wednesday night. Photograph: John Clifton/Action Images/Reuters

blocks.text: Burnham met Carney at a football match in Liverpool on Wednesday night, where the two Everton fans watched their team in the League Cup. Burnham is also due to meet the US president, Donald Trump, for the first time at the UN general assembly in New York next week.

The potential new alliance between the EU and Canada will worry UK ministers that the bloc’s priorities are shifting. Should Burnham fail to complete a food and drink deal that was already on Starmer’s reset agenda, it could have implications for October’s budget, as the economic effects of easing trade with the EU is priced in as part of growth calculations.
The Conservatives criticised the UK/EU reset on Wednesday, saying a future Tory government would build a wholly independent regulatory system.
Alex Burghart, the party’s deputy leader, and Victoria Atkins, the shadow environment secretary, warned the plans would make Britain less competitive.
Speaking at the Policy Exchange thinktank, Burghart said: “Labour’s EU reset is the worst of both worlds and will leave Britain unable to take advantage of our country’s future growth potential.
“The next Conservative government would not be bound by this arrangement and will begin work now on a genuinely independent regulatory system.”

articles.title: Diver injured in great white shark attack off Quebec's Gaspé coast
articles.summary: A diver was transported to hospital after being injured by a great white shark in Percé, Que., in the province’s Gaspé region.

image.caption: According to the Canadian Shark Attack Registry, 15 confirmed shark-related incidents have been recorded in Canada over more than 330 years. (Kirk Yang)

blocks.text: Montreal·New
A diver was transported to hospital after being injured by a great white shark in Percé, Que., in the province’s Gaspé region.
Incident comes amid increase in great white shark sightings in the Gulf of St. Lawrence
According to the Canadian Coast Guard, the incident occurred shortly before 10:30 a.m. on Wednesday.
“Emergency response measures were initiated immediately,” Plongée Percé, a commercial diving firm, said in a Facebook post Wednesday.
“The individual involved received first aid on site before being quickly transported to hospital for further evaluation. We have confirmation that their life is not in danger.”

The Canadian Coast Guard confirms the victim was aboard the vessel Yoda, a Canadian Coast Guard Auxiliary dive boat. As of Wednesday afternoon, the organization was unable to confirm the nature of the victim’s injuries.
On Facebook, Plongée Percé thanked those who helped with the rescue and said it was suspending diving activities for the rest of the season.
Increase in great white sightings
Over the summer, great white shark sightings became more frequent in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and off the coasts of the Gaspé Peninsula and the Magdalen Islands.

Four of these sharks — Webster, Ernst, Bella and Nori — are being tracked by Ocearch, a global non-profit organization that helps scientists study sharks. Nori was spotted south of Anticosti Island, while Ernst and Bella are swimming northeast of the Magdalen Islands.

The organization told CBC News in August that the sighting of Webster off the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador was a sign of a healing ocean. Webster is a 12-foot shark weighing just over 1,000 pounds.

Ocearch founder Chris Fischer said the population of great white sharks was nearly decimated from the 1970s to the 1990s. He said only around nine per cent of the global population remained before efforts were made to protect the remaining population.
Having sharks in the region is a good sign for local fisheries, he said, as sharks instinctively put pressure on seals and ultimately protect fish stocks.

items: Does Nova Scotia need shark-detecting drones?
Shark sightings off northern Newfoundland a welcome sign for researcher

blocks.text: Caroline Miri, a marine biologist with Fisheries and Oceans Canada, said sharks play a key role at the top of the marine food chain.

“They're very important to the health and stability of our oceans and marine ecosystems because these sharks help keep in check some populations of invasive species, and they also control competing fish species lower down on the food chain,” Miri said.
Fischer said Ocearch has tagged around 115 sharks across the Atlantic, from Florida to Newfoundland and Labrador.

According to the St. Lawrence Shark Observatory, the recent increase in sightings of great white sharks in the gulf is mainly due to better documentation and a recovery of the species, which was considered endangered in Canadian waters.
According to the Canadian Shark Attack Registry, 15 confirmed shark-related incidents have been recorded in Canada over more than 330 years.
Written by Isaac Olson, with files from Radio-Canada

articles.title: Trump's Chief of Staff Susie Wiles announces she's cancer-free
articles.summary: The 69-year-old White House chief of staff is a powerful figure and particularly close to the US president.

blocks.text: White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has announced she is free of cancer, exactly six months after she announced her diagnosis.
In a post on X, Wiles said her pathology tests "came back clear" after a visit to the Mayo Clinic earlier this week.
Wiles, 69, is considered among the most powerful figures in the Trump administration and someone particularly close to the US president.
In her post, Wiles thanked Trump for his "unwavering support" and vowed to continue working to "advance his America First Agenda".
Wiles continued working virtually at the White House during the six months of treatment following her diagnosis.
In a March statement, Wiles said that one in eight women are diagnosed with breast cancer.
"Every day, these women continue to raise their families, go to work and serve their communities with strength and determination," she said. "I now join their ranks."
Her post on Wednesday did not reveal any more details about her treatment.
Wiles is the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff - widely considered to be the most important role in the White House.
In her position, Wiles works to keep the president's agenda on track and serves as a gatekeeper to President Trump, as well as a policy coordinator and political advisor.
Before taking the job, Wiles played a significant role in President Trump's 2024 presidential campaign.
Her tenure, however, has not been without controversy.
In December, Vanity Fair published interviews with Wiles in which she gave a blunt - and occasionally unflattering - assessment of her time working in the Trump White House.
For example, she described the famously teetotaling president as having an "alcoholic's personality" but added that there's "nothing he can't do. Nothing, zero, nothing."
She also provided candid thoughts about other figures close to the US president, describing Vice-President JD Vance as a "conspiracy theorist" and Elon Musk as an "odd, odd duck."

The US president, however, swiftly came to her defence and Wiles described Vanity Fair's reporting as having omitted "significant context" to create a "chaotic and negative narrative" about the administration.
President Trump and the White House have yet to comment on Wiles' announcement.

articles.title: Is EU’s offer to Canada a blueprint for Britain – or a reminder it is out in the cold?
articles.summary:
Ursula von der Leyen has opened door for Canada to become associate member to deepen links in ‘openly hostile world’

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has been advocating closer…

blocks.text: Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has been advocating closer alignment with “middle powers” since January in the face of recklessness in Washington.
But what should worry another middle power, the UK, is that it was Brussels that came up with Wednesday’s big reveal in Strasbourg.

To a standing ovation at her State of the Union address, Ursula von der Leyen said she wanted to open the door to Canada becoming the EU’s first “associate member” in a push to forge new ⁠links among allies in “an openly hostile world“.
The European Commission president’s deal could be seen as an “earthquake” offer said Joel Reland, of UK in a Changing Europe, thought it remains “deliciously vague”.
But it also sets Canada apart from the UK, which could, once upon a time, have had some sort of associate membership with the EU were it not for the drive for a clean break Brexit.
The last time associate membership of the EU was mooted was in relation to Ukraine as an off-the-books novel way of bringing Kyiv closer to the bloc without become a fully fledged member state.
New partnerships, von der Leyen said, were needed “in the cold fragility of today’s world” and in the face of an increasingly assertive China.

Just moments earlier she spoke about the need for the EU to diversify urgently its supply of critical raw materials and rare earths currently dominated by China allowing it to follow Japan and stockpile said minerals needed for everything from the car to the defence industries.
It is not a new subject – after all the EU has been grappling with China’s export surplus since 2023 and it introduced the Critical Raw Materials Act as far back as 2024.
The prospect of an enhanced relationship with Ottawa is one that Keir Starmer might have dreamed of.

Canada has something the EU desperately needs – rich supplies of CRM and rare earths – and the EU has something Canada urgently wants: new market for products it can no longer sell into the EU in the face of a trade war with Donald Trump.

Speaking before von der Leyen’s speech, Tobias Cremer, a German social democrat MEP, said a new deeper relationship between the EU and Canada could be a blueprint for other countries, including the UK.

Bernd Lange, the influential chair of the European parliament’s international trade committee, said associate membership could “become a model for close transcontinental partnerships with democratic countries against the new model of the law of the strongest”.

After Iceland’s rejection of membership of the EU, Fabian Zuleeg, the chief executive and chief economist of the European Policy Centre, suggested it was time that the EU developed new models, beyond the European Economic Area, that might offer “partial, gradual or associated membership options”.
after newsletter promotion
Reland said the vagueness of the offer extended to Canada could be promising for the UK’s hopes for a similar offer.

“Any deep Canadian integration into the EU market would take some very heavy work to negotiate a defined set of treaty-bound rights and obligations, and so it seems more likely that – at least in the short term – cooperation will focus on more vaguely constructed alliances for ‘prosperity’ and ‘security’,” which aligns with the UK government’s desires, Reland wrote on Wednesday.

In the current political climate in the UK, it is difficult to envisage a world in which Andy Burnham would encourage any associate membership of the EU. He has a steely focus on domestic issues and it keen to avoid going down any Brexit wormholes.
The UK is seeking a reset with the EU, but the goals in the first year were modest and have yet to be achieved.
The offer to Canada suggests the bigger ambitions for relations with the EU the better.
Additional reporting: Jennifer Rankin
